question_a: Can a party, or the appellate court itself, rely on a factual contention, defence or case that was not pleaded, not made the subject of an issue and not tried in the courts below, when it is raised for the first time on appeal?
question_b: Can a party raise for the first time on appeal (including in the Supreme Court or a second appeal) a contention that depends on disputed or uninvestigated facts, or on a mixed question of law and fact, when it was not pleaded or argued in the courts below?
note: Both rules bar a new contention raised for the first time on appeal when it was not pleaded or urged below and needs factual inquiry (A expressly excepts pure questions of law, and B's triggers exclude them), so they reach consistent outcomes and can be merged.

question_a: When a judge or bench of a High Court (or a smaller bench of the Supreme Court) disagrees with a binding decision of a coordinate or larger bench of the same court, must it follow that decision or refer the question to a larger bench, rather than depart from it or overrule it itself?
question_b: When a bench disagrees with an earlier binding decision of a coordinate or larger bench (or faces conflicting decisions of benches of different strengths), must it follow the earlier decision or refer the matter to a larger bench, rather than depart from it itself?
note: Both rules ask whether a bench must follow or refer an earlier binding decision of a coordinate or larger bench, but Rule A excepts only overruling by a higher court, while Rule B also excepts per incuriam decisions and changes in law, so on those facts A requires following or referring and B does not, a difference explained by an unstated factor rather than a doctrinal shift, since the periods overlap.

question_a: Can a party raise in an appeal (including an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court) a ground, contention or objection that it did not raise, plead, pursue or preserve in the courts below?
question_b: Can a party raise for the first time on appeal (including in the Supreme Court or a second appeal) a contention that depends on disputed or uninvestigated facts, or on a mixed question of law and fact, when it was not pleaded or argued in the courts below?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent subset of Rule A: it covers new appellate contentions that need factual investigation, are mixed questions of law and fact, or contradict the earlier case, which are the non-pure-law grounds Rule A says a court may decline to hear.

question_a: Can a party raise in an appeal (including an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court) a ground, contention or objection that it did not raise, plead, pursue or preserve in the courts below?
question_b: Can a party raise in the Supreme Court (or a higher court in the hierarchy) a plea, contention or objection that was not raised, pleaded, pursued or tried in the courts below, or was abandoned there?
note: Both rules address whether a new ground can be raised for the first time on appeal and reach the same discretionary answer: ordinarily no, unless it is a pure question of law (Rule A) or exceptional circumstances apply (Rule B), so they should be merged.

question_a: Can a party, or the appellate court itself, rely on a factual contention, defence or case that was not pleaded, not made the subject of an issue and not tried in the courts below, when it is raised for the first time on appeal?
question_b: Can a party raise in an appeal (including an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court) a ground, contention or objection that it did not raise, plead, pursue or preserve in the courts below?
note: Rule A is a narrower, stricter application of Rule B's discretionary principle to factual contentions that were unpleaded and untried below, with both rules exempting pure questions of law, so their outcomes are consistent.

question_a: Can a writ challenge to land-acquisition notifications or proceedings be rejected for delay and laches when it is brought after an unreasonable, unexplained lapse of time, although the grounds were available earlier and the acquisition has advanced in the meantime?
question_b: Can a court decline discretionary writ relief against a land acquisition, or a similar public project or approval, because the challenge was brought after substantial and unexplained delay, particularly where the state has acted on the acquisition, third-party rights have arisen or the public would be prejudiced?
note: Both rules let a court reject a delayed, unexplained challenge to a land acquisition for laches, with the same outcome. Rule B generalises this to other public projects and approvals and adds aggravating factors (third-party rights, possession taken, public prejudice), so Rule A reads as the acquisition-specific application of Rule B's principle.

question_a: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
question_b: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
note: Rule A asks whether a separate s.106 termination notice is needed before eviction, while Rule B asks whether a tenant can use relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet against a statutory eviction ground, so they address different questions even though both concern how the Transfer of Property Act interacts with rent-control statutes.

question_a: Is a tenant sued for eviction on the ground of rent default protected from eviction when the tenant has not made the payment, tender or deposit that the rent-control statute requires, in the manner and at the time it requires?
question_b: In an eviction proceeding founded on rent default, does the outcome depend on whether the tenant followed the payment, deposit or demand procedure prescribed by the rent statute, and is the consequence of non-compliance limited to what the statute provides rather than being automatic eviction?
note: Both rules address the consequence of a tenant's non-compliance with statutory payment or deposit procedure, but Rule A treats it as loss of protection leading to eviction while Rule B says the consequence is only what the statute provides (e.g. default status or striking out of the defence) and not automatic eviction; the difference is best explained by statutory wording, such as whether non-compliance forfeits protection outright or only triggers a discretionary consequence, which neither rule states.

question_a: When does a landlord seeking eviction from rented premises for own or family occupation or business use establish a genuine (bona fide) requirement, and what must the landlord prove, including the absence of other suitable accommodation and the link between the claimed user and the landlord's own use?
question_b: When a landlord seeks eviction under a rent-control statute on a ground such as bona fide requirement, rebuilding or demolition, or change of use, must the landlord plead and prove that ground on evidence, with the need assessed objectively on all surrounding circumstances rather than on mere desire or bare assertion?
note: Rule A is the narrower application of Rule B's general requirement (plead and prove the ground, assessed objectively, not on bare assertion) to the personal-need ground, adding the no-suitable-alternative and own/close-family-use elements, and the two give consistent outcomes.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction be sustained when the prosecution's key evidence (eyewitness, sole-witness, dying declaration, approver or confession evidence) is materially unreliable because of contradictions, improvements, interest or hostility, conflict with medical or other evidence, or investigative lapses, and there is no reliable independent corroboration to leave guilt proved beyond reasonable doubt?
question_b: Can a criminal conviction (or a reversal of an acquittal into a conviction) be sustained where the prosecution evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, leaves reasonable doubt about the accused's participation or responsibility?
note: Rule A is a narrower case of Rule B: it applies the general beyond-reasonable-doubt principle in Rule B to convictions resting on materially unreliable key evidence (eyewitness, sole-witness, dying declaration, approver, confession) with no independent corroboration, and both rules give the same outcome of acquittal with the benefit of doubt.

question_a: How must a court determine the market value of compulsorily acquired land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, using comparable-sale evidence, the land's location, potential and condition, and any deductions for development?
question_b: When may sales of small plots be used as comparables to fix the market value of a large acquired tract under the Land Acquisition Act, and what deduction or adjustment for size, development needs and similar factors must be made?
note: Rule B is a narrower case of Rule A, covering the use of small-plot sales as comparables for a large acquired tract and the size and development deduction, which is consistent with Rule A's general requirement to adjust comparables and apply deductions only as circumstances justify.

question_a: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
question_b: Where a court exercises a limited jurisdiction (review, writ/certiorari, supervisory or appellate-on-facts), may it reappraise evidence or reconsider the merits, or must it confine itself to jurisdictional defects and errors apparent on the face of the record?
note: Rule A applies the general limited-jurisdiction principle in Rule B to High Courts in revisional, Art. 226/227 and second-appeal jurisdiction reappraising factual findings, so A is a narrower, consistent case of B.

question_a: Can a party raise for the first time on appeal (including in the Supreme Court or a second appeal) a contention that depends on disputed or uninvestigated facts, or on a mixed question of law and fact, when it was not pleaded or argued in the courts below?
question_b: Can a party raise in the Supreme Court (or a higher court in the hierarchy) a plea, contention or objection that was not raised, pleaded, pursued or tried in the courts below, or was abandoned there?
note: Both rules ask whether a new contention can be raised for the first time on appeal and give the same answer (decline when it needs facts or evidence, is a mixed question, or is a new case), with B only spelling out the abandonment and exceptional-circumstances qualifications that are implicit in A, so they can be merged.

question_a: When does a landlord seeking eviction from rented premises for own or family occupation or business use establish a genuine (bona fide) requirement, and what must the landlord prove, including the absence of other suitable accommodation and the link between the claimed user and the landlord's own use?
question_b: In an eviction claim by a landlord for personal residential or business occupation under a rent control statute, when do the landlord's other accommodation, personal circumstances, or evidentiary gaps defeat or fail to defeat the bona fide and reasonable requirement for the premises?
note: Rule B narrows Rule A's alternative-accommodation element by listing which circumstances do and do not defeat a proven genuine need, and the two give consistent outcomes because both require the alternative to be the landlord's own, available and reasonably suitable.

question_a: Can a party, or the appellate court itself, rely on a factual contention, defence or case that was not pleaded, not made the subject of an issue and not tried in the courts below, when it is raised for the first time on appeal?
question_b: Can a party obtain, at the appellate or later stage, relief, a finding or a remand that depends on a claim that was never pleaded or relief that was never sought, or on evidence that was available but not adduced below, when no recognised ground (amendment, prevention despite due diligence, or need for the court to pronounce judgment) is shown?
note: Both rules apply the principle that a case is decided on what was pleaded and proved below, and Rule A is the narrower application, covering unpleaded and untried factual contentions raised for the first time on appeal, while Rule B is broader, adding unrequested relief and unadduced evidence, with consistent exceptions (pure questions of law in A, and amendment, due diligence or need to pronounce judgment in B).

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: When is a constitutional challenge to a land acquisition, requisition or land-reform law (on grounds such as violation of property rights, colourable legislation, absence of public purpose, or confiscatory deprivation) rejected?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B's 'express constitutional saving' limb (Articles 31(4), 31A and 31B against Part III challenges), while Rule B also covers competence-based challenges and the colourable-legislation limit, and the two never produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: When does an earlier decision, order or proceeding fail to operate as res judicata, constructive res judicata or issue estoppel in a later proceeding?
question_b: Is a later suit or proceeding barred by an earlier one, whether under the rule against splitting claims (Order II Rule 2 CPC), res judicata, or a related procedural bar, when the two arise from distinct causes of action and the later claim or relief was not available or not decided in the earlier proceeding?
note: Both rules only state when a later proceeding is not barred, and Rule B's conditions (distinct causes of action, later relief not available or not finally decided earlier) are a narrower case of Rule A's 'different cause of action' and 'not finally decided' grounds, so they never yield opposite outcomes, even though Rule B also covers the Order II Rule 2 claim-splitting bar and adds the no-omission-without-leave and burden-of-proof qualifications.

question_a: In a suit for possession of immovable property based on title under the Limitation Act, 1963 (Article 65), once the plaintiff proves title, who must prove that adverse possession has defeated it, and is the plaintiff required to prove possession within the preceding twelve years?
question_b: When is a suit or claim for possession not barred by limitation, given that it was filed within the prescribed period counted from dispossession, redemption or the date the defendant's possession began, including after amendment or after an earlier decree became unexecutable?
note: Rule A decides who bears the burden of proving adverse possession once title is proved under Article 65 of the 1963 Act, while Rule B only says a possession suit filed within the period counted from the relevant starting event is not time-barred, so the two address different questions and can both hold without contradiction.

question_a: Can a writ or public interest petition be dismissed or relief refused on the ground of delay and laches where the challenge is brought after substantial, unexplained delay, particularly after the impugned action has become final (for example, award made, possession taken, refund accepted)?
question_b: Can a court decline discretionary writ relief against a land acquisition, or a similar public project or approval, because the challenge was brought after substantial and unexplained delay, particularly where the state has acted on the acquisition, third-party rights have arisen or the public would be prejudiced?
note: Rule B is a narrower application of Rule A, limited to challenges to acquisitions, public projects or approvals and adding aggravating factors (third-party rights, possession and expenditure, public prejudice), while both reach the same permissive outcome that the court may refuse relief for delay and laches.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction (or a reversal of an acquittal into a conviction) be sustained where the prosecution evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, leaves reasonable doubt about the accused's participation or responsibility?
question_b: Must a conviction for an offence founded on group or constructive liability (common intention or unlawful assembly), or on an individual attributed act, be set aside where the evidence does not reliably prove the accused's own participation, shared intention or common object, or where the facts negate the offence, for instance private defence or no death caused?
note: Rule B applies the general reasonable-doubt principle of Rule A to common intention, unlawful assembly, attributed acts, private defence and missing ingredients, so it is a narrower, consistent special case of Rule A.

question_a: Can a protected tenant be evicted, or possession decreed against them, other than through the forum and procedure laid down by the rent-control or tenancy statute and on a statutory ground that the court has found, or has material to find, established?
question_b: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
note: Rule A asks whether a landlord can evict a protected tenant outside the statutory forum and grounds, while Rule B asks whether a tenant can invoke general property-law reliefs against a statutory eviction; the two are consistent because both treat the rent statute as self-contained, but they answer different questions.

question_a: When may an appellate court reverse an acquittal and substitute a conviction, and what standard and reasoning must it satisfy in doing so?
question_b: What limits and standards govern an appellate court's review and reversal of a lower court's findings, particularly an acquittal or findings based on witness credibility, and what must it do before reversing?
note: Rule A is the narrower, consistent application of Rule B's general principle to appeals against acquittal, since both allow reversal only for cogent reasons such as perversity or misread evidence, whereas Rule B also covers witness-credibility and concurrent-findings review.

question_a: When does a litigant or public authority show 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act (or an equivalent power) so that a delay in filing an appeal or similar challenge should be condoned and the matter heard on its merits?
question_b: When may a court condone delay in filing an appeal or other proceeding (including delay in filing required documents or accompanying applications), and when will a higher court interfere with the lower court's exercise of discretion on condonation?
note: Rule A condones delay whenever the explanation is acceptable, there is no gross negligence or mala fides, and substantial justice is served, while Rule B bars condonation if the explanation arose only after limitation expired. The two rules would therefore differ on such facts, and the gap likely reflects unstated differences in context (such as delayed filing of documents or curable defects, and the court's discretion) rather than a doctrinal shift, since the periods overlap.

question_a: Must a first appellate court (or other appellate authority) deciding an appeal on fact and law independently assess the evidence, decide the material issues, and give reasons, engaging with the trial court's reasoning where it reverses, and what is the consequence of failing to do so?
question_b: When may or should an appellate court remand a matter to the court below for determination, and when must it instead decide the appeal itself on the existing record?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B's general remand test, covering a first appellate court that failed to decide material issues or give reasons and so ordinarily warrants remand, while Rule B's 'cannot decide on the existing record' limit is consistent with A's hedged 'ordinarily'.

question_a: When does a tenant's payment, tender or deposit of rent (including a deposit in court or with a rent authority, or a late payment) satisfy the statutory requirement so as to protect the tenant from eviction for rent default?
question_b: When a landlord seeks eviction for rent default under a state rent-control statute, what must a tenant pay or tender, when, and how regularly, to obtain or keep the statutory protection from eviction, and what happens if the tenant falls short?
note: Both rules ask when a tenant's payment protects against eviction for rent default, but Rule A protects a late payment where the court validly extended time while Rule B says courts have no discretion to excuse lateness, and this likely turns on whether the particular state statute empowers courts to extend time, which neither rule states.

question_a: Can a party reopen, in a later appeal, review, execution or fresh proceeding, a decision, finding or order that has already become final or was left unchallenged or was settled earlier between the same parties?
question_b: Once an appealable remand order has gone unappealed, or a prior decision or review has become final, can a court in later proceedings (on remand, in a later appeal, or on review or a post-judgment motion) reopen or re-examine the correctness of that earlier determination directly or indirectly, including through inherent powers?
note: Both rules bar reopening of final or unchallenged determinations, but Rule B is the narrower, consistent application, covering unappealed remand orders, dismissed reviews, and inherent-power or repeat-review routes, and it expressly carves out cases where a statute permits reopening.

question_a: Is an acquisition law, or an acquisition made under it, unconstitutional or invalid merely because it omits compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation that another scheme provides or that the challenger says is required?
question_b: When is a constitutional challenge to a land acquisition, requisition or land-reform law (on grounds such as violation of property rights, colourable legislation, absence of public purpose, or confiscatory deprivation) rejected?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B, covering challenges to acquisition laws based on omitted compensation components, and both reject the challenge when the law is protected or within legislative competence, so their outcomes are consistent.

question_a: In an eviction claim by a landlord for personal residential or business occupation under a rent control statute, when do the landlord's other accommodation, personal circumstances, or evidentiary gaps defeat or fail to defeat the bona fide and reasonable requirement for the premises?
question_b: When a landlord seeks eviction under a rent-control statute on a ground such as bona fide requirement, rebuilding or demolition, or change of use, must the landlord plead and prove that ground on evidence, with the need assessed objectively on all surrounding circumstances rather than on mere desire or bare assertion?
note: Rule B sets the threshold that a landlord must plead and prove the ground objectively, while Rule A asks, once genuine need is already proved on evidence, which other circumstances do or do not defeat it, so the two apply to different stages and do not produce conflicting outcomes.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction rest on credible eyewitness testimony, including testimony from injured, related or partisan witnesses, when it is consistent, carefully scrutinised and corroborated by medical or other evidence, and when discrepancies, relationship, investigative omissions or the accused's injuries are alleged to undermine it?
question_b: When may a court rely on testimony that is inherently suspect or partial (an approver's or accomplice's evidence, a retracted confession, a hostile witness's evidence, or the evidence of an interested or sole witness) to convict an accused, and what scrutiny and corroboration does it require?
note: Rule A applies the same approach (careful scrutiny plus corroboration) to eyewitness evidence, including related, partisan or injured witnesses, which is a narrower subset of the interested-witness evidence covered by Rule B's broader category of suspect or partial testimony, so the two are consistent.

question_a: Can a party, or the appellate court itself, rely on a factual contention, defence or case that was not pleaded, not made the subject of an issue and not tried in the courts below, when it is raised for the first time on appeal?
question_b: Can a party raise in the Supreme Court (or a higher court in the hierarchy) a plea, contention or objection that was not raised, pleaded, pursued or tried in the courts below, or was abandoned there?
note: Both rules govern new pleas raised for the first time on appeal, but they differ on a pure question of law and on exceptional circumstances: A allows a pure legal point needing no inquiry at any stage, while B can decline a new independent legal ground, and B's 'exceptional circumstances' exception could admit an unpleaded factual plea that A would bar. The difference is best explained by unstated factors such as the court's level (first appellate court versus final court) and its discretion.

question_a: When can the government validly invoke urgency powers under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to dispense with the landowner's Section 5A opportunity to object, and what makes such a dispensation invalid?
question_b: When can the Government validly invoke the urgency power under Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to dispense with the Section 5A objection inquiry, and what effect do administrative delay, 'likely to be needed' wording and similar features have on that power?
note: Both rules address when Section 17 urgency can displace the Section 5A hearing, but Rule A (which extends to 2021) applies stricter scrutiny, requiring separate application of mind, material showing real urgency, the land-category condition, and treating prolonged inaction as fatal, whereas Rule B (to 2004) defers to the Government's subjective satisfaction and says administrative delay alone does not defeat the power, so they give different outcomes where there is long delay or the land condition is unmet.

question_a: Can a writ or public interest petition be dismissed or relief refused on the ground of delay and laches where the challenge is brought after substantial, unexplained delay, particularly after the impugned action has become final (for example, award made, possession taken, refund accepted)?
question_b: When a claimant invokes the discretionary writ jurisdiction of a constitutional court after substantial delay, can relief be refused for laches, and what circumstances (explanation for the delay, third-party rights, the nature of the interest) decide the point?
note: Both rules ask whether a court may refuse discretionary writ relief for substantial, unexplained delay and reach the same permissive outcome; A's emphasis on finality and PIL, and B's emphasis on third-party rights and excusable delay, are illustrations of the same principle and can be merged.

question_a: Must a party seeking specific performance (or protection of possession under part performance) plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform its own essential obligations under the contract, and what follows if it does not?
question_b: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, when is a purchaser under an agreement to sell entitled to specific performance, and what must the purchaser plead and prove to show continuous readiness and willingness (financial capacity and conduct)?
note: Rule B is a narrower application of Rule A, limited to a purchaser's specific performance claim under Section 16(c) and adding the Section 20 discretion, while Rule A also covers part-performance protection; both deny relief when readiness and willingness are not pleaded and proved, so they are consistent.

question_a: Can a High Court, in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, set aside concurrent (or first appellate) findings of fact by reappreciating the evidence when no substantial question of law arises and the findings are supported by evidence and not perverse?
question_b: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
note: Rule A (second appeal under Section 100 CPC) is a narrower special case of Rule B, which covers revisional, Article 226/227 and second-appellate jurisdiction and reaches the same outcome: a High Court cannot reappraise supported factual findings absent perversity, legal error or jurisdictional defect.

question_a: When a party to a pending appeal dies and the legal representatives are not substituted within the prescribed time, does the appeal abate, and if so, does the abatement extend only to the deceased party's interest or to the whole appeal?
question_b: When a party to a pending appeal dies (or is wrongly named as a party) and the legal representatives are not substituted, wholly or in part, or in time, does the appeal abate entirely, or does it survive in whole or in part?
note: Both rules address abatement on a party's death without substitution and agree on the divisible versus indivisible split, but where the deceased's estate is already represented on record, or the deceased is a formal or unnecessary party, Rule B lets the appeal proceed while Rule A, as stated, would still abate it as to the deceased and, for joint interests, as to the whole appeal. The difference seems to turn on facts neither rule states in full, such as whether the estate is otherwise represented and the deceased's role in the case.

question_a: Can a writ challenge to land-acquisition notifications or proceedings be rejected for delay and laches when it is brought after an unreasonable, unexplained lapse of time, although the grounds were available earlier and the acquisition has advanced in the meantime?
question_b: Can a writ or public interest petition be dismissed or relief refused on the ground of delay and laches where the challenge is brought after substantial, unexplained delay, particularly after the impugned action has become final (for example, award made, possession taken, refund accepted)?
note: Rule A is the land-acquisition-specific application of Rule B's general principle that a court may refuse relief for substantial, unexplained delay, and the two are consistent, since A's extra conditions (grounds available earlier, acquisition advanced) only narrow the scope.

question_a: Is a land-reform or agrarian-reform law (including acquisition of estates, land-ceiling laws, tenant-ownership laws and amendments to them) immune from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31 (or Part III generally) by virtue of Article 31A, Article 31B/Ninth Schedule or related provisions, and what conditions must be met for that immunity, such as presidential assent for a State law?
question_b: When is a land-reform or resource-distribution law (or the constitutional amendment protecting it) immune from challenge under the equality, freedom and property provisions of the Constitution, and what connection to agrarian reform or to distribution of material resources for the common good is needed for that immunity?
note: Rule A treats Ninth Schedule listing or Article 31A protection as a bar to Part III challenges, while Rule B, which also covers Article 31C-type resource distribution and basic structure review, requires a real nexus to agrarian reform or the common good, so a scheduled law lacking that nexus would be immune under A but open to challenge under B (as in the later post-Kesavananda and I.R. Coelho line).

question_a: When does a tenant's payment, tender or deposit of rent (including a deposit in court or with a rent authority, or a late payment) satisfy the statutory requirement so as to protect the tenant from eviction for rent default?
question_b: When a tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears in the manner or within the time the statute, the court or the landlord's accepted practice allows, can the landlord still obtain eviction for rent default?
note: Both rules ask when payment protects a tenant from default eviction, but Rule A's statement treats a late payment without a court extension as default, while Rule B protects a tenant where the landlord's long unprotested acceptance of irregular payments shows no habitual default; the difference likely turns on the type of statutory default ground (a single default after notice versus habitual or wilful default), which neither rule states, and the overlapping decision periods (1963-1995 and 1964-2022) argue against a doctrinal shift.

question_a: When may a High Court, in second appeal (or analogous revision), interfere with or reappraise the factual findings of the lower courts, including concurrent findings, and when must it leave them undisturbed?
question_b: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
note: Both rules address the same question, whether a High Court may disturb concurrent or supported factual findings in second appeal or revision. They give consistent, complementary answers: interference is allowed only for perversity, misreading or ignoring material evidence, or legal error, and is barred where the finding is merely open to a different view. Rule B is only a broader framing that adds Art. 226/227.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: Is a land-reform or agrarian-reform law (including acquisition of estates, land-ceiling laws, tenant-ownership laws and amendments to them) immune from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31 (or Part III generally) by virtue of Article 31A, Article 31B/Ninth Schedule or related provisions, and what conditions must be met for that immunity, such as presidential assent for a State law?
note: Both rules bar Part III challenges to estate-acquisition and agrarian-reform laws and to Ninth Schedule laws, but Rule B adds conditions that Rule A omits (presidential assent for unscheduled State laws, and a genuine agrarian-reform scheme), so an unscheduled State estate law without assent is protected under A as written but not under B, a difference explained by the Article 31A proviso rather than by any real disagreement between the cases.

question_a: Must a first appellate court (or other appellate authority) deciding an appeal on fact and law independently assess the evidence, decide the material issues, and give reasons, engaging with the trial court's reasoning where it reverses, and what is the consequence of failing to do so?
question_b: What limits and standards govern an appellate court's review and reversal of a lower court's findings, particularly an acquittal or findings based on witness credibility, and what must it do before reversing?
note: Rule A sets the general duty of an appellate court to assess the evidence independently, give reasons and engage with the trial court's reasoning before reversing, while Rule B adds a narrower, consistent standard for reversing acquittals and credibility-based or concurrent findings, which requires giving due weight to the trial court's view and showing cogent reasons.

question_a: When is a constitutional challenge to a land acquisition, requisition or land-reform law (on grounds such as violation of property rights, colourable legislation, absence of public purpose, or confiscatory deprivation) rejected?
question_b: When does a constitutional property-based challenge to the compensation or amount payable under a land-ceiling or land-acquisition law fail, whether under Article 31(2), the second proviso to Article 31A(1) or Article 31B?
note: Rule B is a narrower sub-case of Rule A, covering only compensation challenges to land-ceiling or acquisition laws, and its grounds (scheduled-law immunity under Art. 31B, non-application of the proviso, non-illusory amount) fit within A's general approach, so the two give consistent outcomes.

question_a: Is an acquisition law, or an acquisition made under it, unconstitutional or invalid merely because it omits compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation that another scheme provides or that the challenger says is required?
question_b: When does a constitutional property-based challenge to the compensation or amount payable under a land-ceiling or land-acquisition law fail, whether under Article 31(2), the second proviso to Article 31A(1) or Article 31B?
note: Rule A asks whether omitting compensation components (solatium, interest, rehabilitation) invalidates an acquisition law, while Rule B asks when a challenge to the amount of compensation under Articles 31(2), 31A or 31B fails; they share a theme and a shield-type exception, but both only say challenges fail on different conditions, so no facts produce opposite outcomes.

question_a: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
question_b: When a landlord or authority proceeds for eviction on a particular statutory ground or under a special statutory procedure, is it excused from satisfying a further prerequisite or protection (such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of title, a rehousing duty or tenant-protection law) because that requirement is not part of the invoked ground or is displaced by the invoked scheme?
note: Rule A is a notice-specific application of Rule B's idea, but where a rent statute only restricts eviction and preserves the contractual or s.106 notice (or the contractual tenancy still subsists), Rule A still requires notice while Rule B's 'not part of the invoked ground' limb would excuse it, and the difference turns on whether the statute displaces or preserves the notice requirement, which Rule B does not state.

question_a: What is the effect under the doctrine of lis pendens (Section 52, Transfer of Property Act) of a transfer of immovable property made by a party while litigation directly concerning that property is pending: is the transfer void, or valid but subject to the rights determined in the litigation?
question_b: Is a person who acquires an interest in property from a party while litigation concerning that property is pending bound by the final outcome of that litigation (lis pendens), even though the transfer is not void and no interim order restrained it?
note: Both rules apply s.52 TPA to say a pendente lite transfer is not void but the transferee takes subject to the litigation's final outcome, and A's extra conditions (non-collusive suit, party transferor) are standard elements of the doctrine that don't change the result, so they can be merged.

question_a: Once possession of land has been taken under an acquisition (or the statutory vesting event has occurred) and the land has vested absolutely in the State free from encumbrances, can that vesting be undone by withdrawal, release, lapse for delayed award, later legislation or later orders, or by the former owner's claim to restoration?
question_b: Once land or a proprietary or intermediary interest in it has vested in the State (by completed acquisition or by land-reform, ceiling or surplus legislation), can the former owner or proprietor recover possession, restitution, reconveyance or related relief, or does the vesting bar the claim?
note: Both rules deny the former owner relief once land has validly vested in the State, subject to a statutory exception (a revesting mechanism in A, a saving or reconveyance condition in B), so they never give opposite outcomes; Rule A is the narrower acquisition-specific application (possession taken, plus withdrawal, lapse and later-law arguments), while Rule B is the broader principle that also covers land-reform, ceiling and proprietary-interest vesting.

question_a: When does an earlier decision, order or proceeding fail to operate as res judicata, constructive res judicata or issue estoppel in a later proceeding?
question_b: Does an earlier decree, order or judgment (especially a consent or compromise decree, or an order that reserves the merits or does not decide the point) bind the parties or later courts, by res judicata, estoppel or precedent, on an issue that the earlier court did not actually adjudicate?
note: Rule B (an earlier decree or order does not bind on an issue the court never adjudicated, including consent decrees and orders reserving the merits) is a narrower application of Rule A's first limb, that res judicata fails where the matter was not directly and substantially in issue and finally decided, so the two never give different outcomes. Rule A is broader because it adds other exceptions: different parties, property or cause of action, and pure questions of law or jurisdiction.

question_a: When may a court allow amendment of a pleading (especially a written statement) under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, notwithstanding delay, an alternative or inconsistent plea, an explained admission or a possible limitation bar, and what conditions such as absence of serious prejudice or costs govern the exercise of that discretion?
question_b: When may a court permit amendment of a pleading in a pending civil proceeding under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, in particular where the amendment supplies particulars, adds or alters relief, or is sought after limitation has expired, without changing the nature of the suit or causing irremediable prejudice?
note: Both rules address liberal amendment of pleadings under Order VI Rule 17 CPC: amendment is allowed when needed to decide the real controversy, absent a new cause of action or change in the nature of the case, withdrawal of an admission, or prejudice that costs cannot cure, and delay or limitation alone does not bar it. The differences (written statement versus plaint focus, and B's pretrial or due-diligence qualifier) are differences of emphasis, not contradictory outcomes, so the rules can be merged.

question_a: When does a tenant's payment, tender or deposit of rent (including a deposit in court or with a rent authority, or a late payment) satisfy the statutory requirement so as to protect the tenant from eviction for rent default?
question_b: In an eviction proceeding founded on rent default, does the outcome depend on whether the tenant followed the payment, deposit or demand procedure prescribed by the rent statute, and is the consequence of non-compliance limited to what the statute provides rather than being automatic eviction?
note: Both rules treat statutory compliance as decisive for rent-default protection, and Rule B refines Rule A's non-compliance branch by saying the consequence is only the statutory default consequence (such as default status or striking out of the defence) and not automatic eviction.

question_a: When may an appellate court reverse or interfere with an acquittal, and must it leave the acquittal undisturbed where the trial court's view of the evidence is reasonable or possible and the evidence permits two views?
question_b: What limits and standards govern an appellate court's review and reversal of a lower court's findings, particularly an acquittal or findings based on witness credibility, and what must it do before reversing?
note: Rule A is the acquittal-specific application of Rule B, which sets the same deference-unless-perversity-or-compelling-reasons standard for acquittals and also for witness-credibility and concurrent-findings review, so the two are consistent and A is the narrower case.

question_a: When may a court condone delay in filing an appeal or other proceeding (including delay in filing required documents or accompanying applications), and when will a higher court interfere with the lower court's exercise of discretion on condonation?
question_b: When may a court or authority condone a delay (or a failure to meet a procedural time limit) in filing a proceeding, and on what showing of sufficient cause, such as bona fide pursuit of another remedy or an explained delay?
note: Both rules govern condonation of delay on sufficient cause, but A bars condonation where the explanation arose only after limitation expired and also allows it where the court permitted later filing or the defect is curable, while B has no such bar and instead allows bona fide pursuit of another remedy and directory time limits, so outcomes diverge on some facts; the likely explanation is an unstated difference in context (appeals under a statute with strict limitation versus proceedings before forums with directory limits), not a doctrinal shift, since the date ranges overlap.

question_a: In an eviction claim by a landlord for personal residential or business occupation under a rent control statute, when do the landlord's other accommodation, personal circumstances, or evidentiary gaps defeat or fail to defeat the bona fide and reasonable requirement for the premises?
question_b: Where premises are let for both residential and non-residential (professional or business) purposes, or a residential letting is openly used for non-residential purposes with the landlord's consent, can the landlord evict on a ground that depends on the premises being residential (landlord's residential need, or tenant's acquisition of other residence)?
note: Rule A asks whether the landlord's other accommodation or personal circumstances defeat a proven bona fide need, while Rule B asks whether a residence-based ground is available at all given the purpose of the letting, so they address separate issues and are not contradictory because Rule A's outcome is limited to 'not defeated by the alleged circumstance'.

question_a: Can a High Court, in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, set aside concurrent (or first appellate) findings of fact by reappreciating the evidence when no substantial question of law arises and the findings are supported by evidence and not perverse?
question_b: Can a High Court decide a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in particular by reappreciating evidence and reversing the factual findings of the courts below, without first formulating a substantial question of law and hearing the appeal on that question?
note: Both rules enforce the Section 100 limit that a High Court may decide a second appeal only on a substantial question of law, and Rule A (no reappreciation to reverse supported, non-perverse concurrent findings when no such question arises) is a narrower, consistent application of Rule B's broader requirement that the question be formulated and the appeal decided on it.

question_a: Can a party reopen, in a later appeal, review, execution or fresh proceeding, a decision, finding or order that has already become final or was left unchallenged or was settled earlier between the same parties?
question_b: Can a matter already finally decided between the parties, by a court or authority with jurisdiction, be reopened or re-agitated in later proceedings (execution, remand, repeated administrative proceedings or fresh applications) in which the earlier decision is binding?
note: Both rules bar reopening an issue already finally decided between the same parties in later proceedings, and they differ only in emphasis (Rule A adds failure to challenge and limited-review restraint, Rule B adds execution and remand settings and the new-cause-of-action exception), so they can be merged without any outcome conflict.

question_a: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
question_b: When may an appellate, revisional or supervisory court (including the Supreme Court under Article 136) interfere with a lower court's discretionary decision, and when must it leave that decision undisturbed?
note: Rule A concerns a High Court's power under limited non-appellate jurisdiction to reappraise a lower forum's factual findings, while Rule B concerns when a higher court may interfere with a lower court's discretionary order; both reflect restraint with a perversity exception, but they address different subject matter and neither narrows or contradicts the other.

question_a: Can a High Court, in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, set aside concurrent (or first appellate) findings of fact by reappreciating the evidence when no substantial question of law arises and the findings are supported by evidence and not perverse?
question_b: When may the Supreme Court, hearing an appeal (typically by special leave under Article 136), disturb concurrent findings of fact reached by the trial court and the appellate or High Court?
note: Rule A limits a High Court's power under Section 100 CPC to reappreciate evidence in a second appeal, while Rule B limits the Supreme Court's discretionary power under Article 136 to disturb concurrent findings; the principles are parallel and consistent, but the courts, jurisdictional sources, and questions differ.

question_a: Is a court or rent controller bound to strike out a tenant's defence automatically whenever the tenant fails to pay or deposit rent as ordered in an eviction proceeding, or does it have discretion to retain the defence and condone the default, and when should that discretion be exercised for or against the tenant?
question_b: In an eviction proceeding founded on rent default, does the outcome depend on whether the tenant followed the payment, deposit or demand procedure prescribed by the rent statute, and is the consequence of non-compliance limited to what the statute provides rather than being automatic eviction?
note: Both rules agree that non-compliance with payment or deposit requirements does not automatically lead to eviction; Rule A is the narrower case, saying that when the consequence is striking out the defence for breach of a payment order, that power is discretionary and penal, which fits within Rule B's broader principle that the consequence is limited to what the statute provides.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: Is an acquisition law, or an acquisition made under it, unconstitutional or invalid merely because it omits compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation that another scheme provides or that the challenger says is required?
note: Rule B's 'constitutional shield' branch is essentially Rule A applied to compensation-omission challenges, so Rule A explains one branch of the broader Rule B and the two give consistent outcomes.

question_a: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
question_b: Does a landlord's acceptance of rent or equivalent payments after a lease or tenancy has expired or been terminated create a new tenancy by holding over, or waive a termination notice or eviction ground, in the absence of the landlord's clear assent to continued possession or intention to treat the lease as subsisting?
note: Rule A asks when a separate termination notice is required or dispensed with, while Rule B asks whether accepting rent after expiry or termination shows assent to holding over or waives notice; the two are complementary (B informs A's 'no assent to holding over' element) and never yield conflicting outcomes.

question_a: When may an appellate court reverse an acquittal and substitute a conviction, and what standard and reasoning must it satisfy in doing so?
question_b: Must a first appellate court (or other appellate authority) deciding an appeal on fact and law independently assess the evidence, decide the material issues, and give reasons, engaging with the trial court's reasoning where it reverses, and what is the consequence of failing to do so?
note: Rule A applies Rule B's general duty (independent reappraisal, reasons, engaging the trial court's reasoning) to appeals against acquittal and adds a stricter substantive threshold for reversal (perversity or misread evidence, not merely another possible view), with no inconsistency in outcomes.

question_a: When does a tenant's denial or challenge of the landlord's title (or of the tenancy) in a rent-control eviction proceeding furnish a ground for eviction, and how far may the rent-control forum inquire into the denial without finally deciding title?
question_b: In a summary eviction proceeding where the tenant must obtain leave to contest or defend, when must the Controller or court grant leave, and when may it refuse leave?
note: Rule A is a substantive rule on when a tenant's denial of title is itself a ground for eviction, while Rule B is a procedural rule on when a tenant must be granted leave to contest in summary eviction, so they answer different questions and can be applied together without conflict.

question_a: When may a High Court, in second appeal (or analogous revision), interfere with or reappraise the factual findings of the lower courts, including concurrent findings, and when must it leave them undisturbed?
question_b: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, when may the Supreme Court depart from its ordinary restraint and interfere with, or reappraise, findings of fact, including concurrent findings of the courts below?
note: Rule A governs a High Court's power in second appeal or revision, which turns on a substantial question of law, while Rule B governs the Supreme Court's discretionary power under Article 136, which turns on manifest injustice; the forums and thresholds differ, so they are parallel but distinct rules, not merged, narrowed, or conflicting.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction (or a reversal of an acquittal into a conviction) be sustained where the prosecution evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, leaves reasonable doubt about the accused's participation or responsibility?
question_b: Is an accused entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt (so that an acquittal is upheld or restored, or a conviction set aside) where the prosecution's evidence of that accused's participation in the charged offence is unreliable, contradictory, uncorroborated or in conflict with medical, ballistic or recovery evidence?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent application of Rule A's general benefit-of-doubt principle, limited to unreliable or uncorroborated evidence of participation (contradictory eyewitnesses, conflict with medical or forensic evidence, unproved recoveries or identification, no overt act), whereas Rule A also covers incomplete circumstantial chains and other insufficiency.

question_a: When does a litigant or public authority show 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act (or an equivalent power) so that a delay in filing an appeal or similar challenge should be condoned and the matter heard on its merits?
question_b: When may a court or authority condone a delay (or a failure to meet a procedural time limit) in filing a proceeding, and on what showing of sufficient cause, such as bona fide pursuit of another remedy or an explained delay?
note: Rule A is the narrower, Section 5 Limitation Act application of the general condonation principle in Rule B, adding the safeguard that gross negligence, deliberate inaction or mala fides defeat sufficient cause, while Rule B extends to directory time limits, bona fide pursuit of another remedy and condonation without a formal application, so the two are consistent.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: When a competent legislature retrospectively validates earlier acts (acquisitions, vestings, evictions) that were defective or made under a repealed or invalid law, does the validation sustain those acts against challenges based on the cured defect, such as a missing procedural step, a prior court order, a repealed law, or discrimination between procedures?
note: Rule A asks whether estate-reform or Ninth Schedule laws are immune from Part III fundamental-rights challenges, while Rule B asks whether retrospective validation cures a specific procedural or legal defect in past acts, so they address distinct questions and can operate together without producing contradictory outcomes.

question_a: When may an appellate court reverse an acquittal and substitute a conviction, and what standard and reasoning must it satisfy in doing so?
question_b: When may a High Court, in second appeal (or analogous revision), interfere with or reappraise the factual findings of the lower courts, including concurrent findings, and when must it leave them undisturbed?
note: Rule A governs when an appellate court may reverse an acquittal in a criminal appeal, while Rule B governs when a High Court may interfere with factual findings in a civil second appeal or analogous revision; the two share a perversity/misreading-of-evidence idea, but they address different questions in different procedural settings.

question_a: When may a High Court, in second appeal (or analogous revision), interfere with or reappraise the factual findings of the lower courts, including concurrent findings, and when must it leave them undisturbed?
question_b: Can a High Court decide a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in particular by reappreciating evidence and reversing the factual findings of the courts below, without first formulating a substantial question of law and hearing the appeal on that question?
note: Rule A states the substantive grounds on which a High Court may disturb factual findings, namely defects that raise a substantial question of law, while Rule B adds the procedural precondition that such a question be formulated and heard first, so the two are consistent and B narrows how A's power is exercised.

question_a: Is a law included in the Ninth Schedule protected by Article 31B from invalidation on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges, fundamental rights in Part III (including the property guarantee carried over from the former constitutional order), and does that protection extend to earlier amendments and operate retrospectively?
question_b: Is a land-reform or agrarian-reform law (including acquisition of estates, land-ceiling laws, tenant-ownership laws and amendments to them) immune from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31 (or Part III generally) by virtue of Article 31A, Article 31B/Ninth Schedule or related provisions, and what conditions must be met for that immunity, such as presidential assent for a State law?
note: Rule B is the narrower land-reform application of the same Article 31A/31B immunity that Rule A states generally for Ninth Schedule laws, and both bar Part III challenges in the overlapping cases (scheduled land laws), so they are consistent.

question_a: Is a tenant (or a person claiming through the tenant) who was let into possession by, or has attorned to, a landlord barred from denying that landlord's title, or from setting up adverse possession against it, while the tenancy continues and possession has not been surrendered?
question_b: When does a tenant's denial or challenge of the landlord's title (or of the tenancy) in a rent-control eviction proceeding furnish a ground for eviction, and how far may the rent-control forum inquire into the denial without finally deciding title?
note: Rule A asks whether a tenant is estopped from denying the landlord's title or claiming adverse possession, while Rule B asks when a title denial is an eviction ground in rent-control proceedings, so they have different outcome variables and do not contradict each other even though their exceptions (derivative title, vitiated attornment, bona fide dispute) are related.

question_a: Is a tenant sued for eviction on the ground of rent default protected from eviction when the tenant has not made the payment, tender or deposit that the rent-control statute requires, in the manner and at the time it requires?
question_b: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
note: Rule A asks whether a tenant who misses the statutory payment, tender or deposit requirements keeps the statute's protection, while Rule B asks whether general property-law reliefs (relief against forfeiture, a default right to sublet) can supplement the statute; the two are complementary and consistent, and neither narrows the other.

question_a: When may or should an appellate court remand a matter to the court below for determination, and when must it instead decide the appeal itself on the existing record?
question_b: When may or must an appellate court decide an appeal or determine the disputed relief itself on the available record instead of remanding the matter to the lower court?
note: Both rules answer when an appellate court should remand versus decide on the existing record, and they are complementary: A remands only when the record is insufficient and the court cannot decide, while B decides when the record permits and no retrial or fresh evidence is needed, so they never yield different outcomes on the same facts and can be merged.

question_a: In a rent-control eviction proceeding founded on the landlord's bona fide need, how must the court decide the statutory limits on eviction (comparative hardship, tenant protection, partial eviction and related relief) once the need is established, and what must it consider before ordering full eviction?
question_b: When a landlord seeks eviction under a rent-control statute on a ground such as bona fide requirement, rebuilding or demolition, or change of use, must the landlord plead and prove that ground on evidence, with the need assessed objectively on all surrounding circumstances rather than on mere desire or bare assertion?
note: Rule B governs whether the landlord has pleaded and proved the eviction ground, while Rule A governs what the court must decide (comparative hardship, partial eviction, tenant protection) after the need is established, so they apply at sequential stages and cannot yield opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: When does a tenant's payment, tender or deposit of rent (including a deposit in court or with a rent authority, or a late payment) satisfy the statutory requirement so as to protect the tenant from eviction for rent default?
question_b: Is a court or rent controller bound to strike out a tenant's defence automatically whenever the tenant fails to pay or deposit rent as ordered in an eviction proceeding, or does it have discretion to retain the defence and condone the default, and when should that discretion be exercised for or against the tenant?
note: Rule A asks whether a payment or deposit satisfies the statutory requirement and protects the tenant from eviction on the ground of default, while Rule B asks whether failure to comply with a court's rent-payment order automatically leads to striking out the defence, and the two do not give inconsistent outcomes (Rule A even accepts a court-granted extension, which is consistent with Rule B's discretion to condone).

question_a: Does a law or grant condition that restricts, regulates or retrospectively affects property rights (by limiting transfers, evictions, rents or recovery of possession) infringe the constitutional property guarantees (Articles 19(1)(f), 31, 31A) when it is a reasonable measure serving a public purpose, or when the claimant's interest was defeasible or merely regulated rather than acquired?
question_b: Is a special or summary statutory procedure affecting tenants' or occupants' possession and property rights (eviction, clearance or redevelopment) constitutionally valid under Articles 14 and 19 where it rests on a reasonable classification or public purpose and gives affected persons notice, an opportunity to object or defend, and review or appeal safeguards?
note: Rule A asks whether a substantive restriction on property is a reasonable regulation rather than an infringement of the property guarantees (Arts. 19(1)(f), 31, 31A), while Rule B asks whether a special or summary possession procedure is valid under Arts. 14 and 19 given its classification and procedural safeguards, so the questions differ even though both concern landlord-tenant and possession laws and both uphold the measure.

question_a: When does a final decision on an issue in an earlier suit or proceeding, made by a court competent to decide it, bar relitigation of that issue between the same parties or their privies in a later suit or proceeding?
question_b: Does a final decision on the merits by a competent court or tribunal, including in a constitutional writ proceeding or quasi-judicial proceeding that is not itself a suit, bar the same parties or their privies from relitigating the same issue or matter in a later proceeding?
note: Both state the same res judicata bar (competent forum, final decision, same parties or privies, same issue directly decided), but Rule B extends it to writ courts and quasi-judicial tribunals and so covers a wider set of forums than Rule A's court-focused rule, with no difference in outcome on any shared facts.

question_a: When a rent-control or tenancy law is enacted, amended, repealed or expires, does its protection (or the withdrawal of protection) apply to eviction proceedings, tenancies or defaults that predate it or are pending when it takes effect, or is the matter governed by the earlier or general law?
question_b: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
note: Rule A asks whether a change in rent-control law applies prospectively or to earlier or pending proceedings (temporal scope), while Rule B asks whether a tenant can invoke general property-law protections against a statutory eviction ground (the statute's self-contained nature), so the two address distinct questions and cannot produce opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction be sustained when the prosecution's key evidence (eyewitness, sole-witness, dying declaration, approver or confession evidence) is materially unreliable because of contradictions, improvements, interest or hostility, conflict with medical or other evidence, or investigative lapses, and there is no reliable independent corroboration to leave guilt proved beyond reasonable doubt?
question_b: Must a conviction for an offence founded on group or constructive liability (common intention or unlawful assembly), or on an individual attributed act, be set aside where the evidence does not reliably prove the accused's own participation, shared intention or common object, or where the facts negate the offence, for instance private defence or no death caused?
note: Both rules set aside convictions where guilt is not reliably proved and no independent evidence fills the gap, with no outcome conflict; Rule B applies this to proof of the accused's own role, common intention or common object and adds substantive defeaters (private defence, missing ingredient), so it is a specialised, consistent case of Rule A's general unreliable-evidence principle.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: Is a law included in the Ninth Schedule protected by Article 31B from invalidation on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges, fundamental rights in Part III (including the property guarantee carried over from the former constitutional order), and does that protection extend to earlier amendments and operate retrospectively?
note: Rule B restates and elaborates the Ninth Schedule/Article 31B branch of Rule A (protection of scheduled laws, including earlier amendments and retrospective effect), while Rule A is broader because it also covers estate-acquisition laws under Articles 31(4) and 31A, and the outcomes are consistent.

question_a: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
question_b: Is judicial review of an administrative, quasi-judicial or disciplinary decision confined to the legality and fairness of the decision-making process, so that a court or tribunal may not reappraise the evidence or substitute its own view on the merits where the decision is supported by the record and no reviewable defect is shown?
note: Rule A is a narrower, consistent application of Rule B's general principle that review is limited to legality and process rather than merits, applied specifically to High Courts exercising revisional, supervisory or second-appellate jurisdiction over factual findings, with matching grounds for intervention (perversity, no evidence, legal error, jurisdictional defect).

question_a: When an earlier land-acquisition declaration has been quashed, set aside, cancelled or held invalid, can a fresh declaration be made on the same preliminary notification, and does that depend on whether it falls within the statutory period running from that notification?
question_b: Does delay or an interval in the steps of a land acquisition (between the preliminary notification, its publication or local notice, the declaration and its publication, or the completion of proceedings) invalidate the acquisition, absent proof that the statutory deadline was missed for the act the statute actually regulates or evidence of bad faith?
note: Rule A asks whether a fresh declaration can follow an invalidated one on the same preliminary notification, while Rule B asks whether delay between acquisition steps invalidates the acquisition; they touch the same time limit but do not give conflicting outcomes, since B only applies where the statutory deadline was not breached, which is consistent with A's requirement that a fresh declaration fall within the original period.

question_a: When a law authorising compulsory acquisition or requisition of property is challenged on the ground that its compensation is inadequate or illusory, is the challenge open to judicial review, and what must the compensation provisions satisfy to survive it?
question_b: When does a constitutional property-based challenge to the compensation or amount payable under a land-ceiling or land-acquisition law fail, whether under Article 31(2), the second proviso to Article 31A(1) or Article 31B?
note: Rule B applies Rule A's logic (saving or scheduled immunity, or relevant and non-illusory compensation, so the challenge fails and inadequacy alone is no ground) to the narrower setting of land-ceiling and acquisition laws under Articles 31(2), 31A and 31B, and adds ceiling-specific routes (superseded ceiling, proviso not attracted) without producing a contrary outcome.

question_a: Does eyewitness testimony in a criminal case have to be rejected because of minor or collateral discrepancies, omissions in the first report, delay, relationship of the witnesses, absence of independent or forensic corroboration, or medical evidence that does not wholly exclude the account?
question_b: Can a court reject a witness's testimony merely because the witness is related to the victim or to the party calling the witness, or is otherwise interested, or must the testimony be scrutinised on its merits?
note: Rule B sets out in detail one ground that Rule A lists among several (relationship or interest of the witness), and both reach the same outcome of no rejection on that ground alone if the testimony is credible, so they are consistent and B works as a specific application of A's broader principle.

question_a: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
question_b: Can a protected tenant be evicted, or possession decreed against them, other than through the forum and procedure laid down by the rent-control or tenancy statute and on a statutory ground that the court has found, or has material to find, established?
note: Rule A asks whether a separate termination notice is needed before eviction, while Rule B asks whether a protected tenant can be evicted outside the statutory forum and grounds; A's 'notice not required' outcome does not say eviction is available, so it never contradicts B's limits.

question_a: Where a land ceiling law makes a statutorily defined family the unit for applying the ceiling, must land held by each family member (including separated minor sons and spouses holding separately) be aggregated into the family's holding, and is that family-unit approach constitutionally valid?
question_b: Where land is held by or in the name of one member of a joint family, or is former watan land, does a separate holding, commutation of services, abolition or a partition of other property alter its character as family property, so that the member, share or land is counted with the family (or remains joint family property) rather than being treated as separate property or a separate unit?
note: Rule B is the general default that a member's separate name or holding does not take land out of the family unit unless separateness is proved or a statute says otherwise, and Rule A is the narrower statutory ceiling-law case in which the statute itself fixes the family as the unit and aggregates even separately held land, so the two are consistent.

question_a: Is a court or rent controller bound to strike out a tenant's defence automatically whenever the tenant fails to pay or deposit rent as ordered in an eviction proceeding, or does it have discretion to retain the defence and condone the default, and when should that discretion be exercised for or against the tenant?
question_b: When a tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears in the manner or within the time the statute, the court or the landlord's accepted practice allows, can the landlord still obtain eviction for rent default?
note: Rule A decides whether a defence may be struck out for breaching a payment or deposit order (a procedural sanction), while Rule B decides whether a tenant who has validly cured the arrears can still be evicted for rent default (a substantive ground), so they address different questions and do not yield contradictory outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Under rent-control legislation, when does a tenant's act (subletting without the required consent, use contrary to the lease, or construction or alteration of the premises) establish a statutory ground for eviction, and what must the landlord prove?
question_b: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
note: Rule A asks whether a tenant's act and the landlord's proof establish a statutory eviction ground, while Rule B asks whether a separate notice terminating the tenancy is needed; B only uses an established ground as one precondition, so the rules are complementary and cannot produce different outcomes on the same question.

question_a: Can a party raise in an appeal (including an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court) a ground, contention or objection that it did not raise, plead, pursue or preserve in the courts below?
question_b: Can a party obtain, at the appellate or later stage, relief, a finding or a remand that depends on a claim that was never pleaded or relief that was never sought, or on evidence that was available but not adduced below, when no recognised ground (amendment, prevention despite due diligence, or need for the court to pronounce judgment) is shown?
note: Rule B is a narrower, stricter application of Rule A's general principle: it covers unpleaded claims, unrequested relief and unadduced evidence, where refusal is mandatory absent a recognised ground, while Rule A covers all new grounds and leaves refusal discretionary, with a pure-question-of-law exception.

question_a: Can a court decline discretionary writ relief against a land acquisition, or a similar public project or approval, because the challenge was brought after substantial and unexplained delay, particularly where the state has acted on the acquisition, third-party rights have arisen or the public would be prejudiced?
question_b: When a claimant invokes the discretionary writ jurisdiction of a constitutional court after substantial delay, can relief be refused for laches, and what circumstances (explanation for the delay, third-party rights, the nature of the interest) decide the point?
