question_b: Can a court (reference court or civil court) determine or enhance compensation for acquired land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when no valid reference on compensation has been made to it under Section 18, and can that defect be cured by acquiescence, a later clarification, or an ordinary suit?
note: Rule A concerns the merits and evidentiary burden for enhancing compensation, while Rule B concerns the court's jurisdiction, which depends on a valid Section 18 reference; the two can apply together and never produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: Can a High Court, in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, set aside concurrent (or first appellate) findings of fact by reappreciating the evidence when no substantial question of law arises and the findings are supported by evidence and not perverse?
question_b: Where a court exercises a limited jurisdiction (review, writ/certiorari, supervisory or appellate-on-facts), may it reappraise evidence or reconsider the merits, or must it confine itself to jurisdictional defects and errors apparent on the face of the record?
note: Rule A is a narrower special case of Rule B: a High Court's second appeal under Section 100 CPC is a restricted appellate jurisdiction, and A's conditions (no substantial question of law, findings supported by evidence and not perverse) correspond to B's 'no perversity, patent error of law or jurisdictional defect' conditions, so both give the same outcome that the lower findings stand.

question_a: When a party to a pending appeal dies (or is wrongly named as a party) and the legal representatives are not substituted, wholly or in part, or in time, does the appeal abate entirely, or does it survive in whole or in part?
question_b: Can a person who succeeds to or claims through a party's interest in the subject matter of a pending appeal (by assignment, transfer, devolution or succession) be brought on record to continue or defend the appeal, even where the formal procedure for substitution was not followed or was incorrectly invoked?
note: Rule A asks whether an appeal abates, in whole or in part, when a party dies and no one is substituted, while Rule B asks whether a successor or assignee of a party's interest may be brought on record to continue or defend the appeal, so the two are complementary and do not produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: When is a constitutional challenge to a land acquisition, requisition or land-reform law (on grounds such as violation of property rights, colourable legislation, absence of public purpose, or confiscatory deprivation) rejected?
question_b: Is a special acquisition, town-planning or improvement scheme invalid under the equality guarantee (Article 14) merely because its procedure, compensation method or review mechanism differs from the general land-acquisition law, or because another acquisition law could theoretically be used?
note: Rule A decides challenges based on legislative competence, colourable legislation and express constitutional savings, while Rule B decides a distinct Article 14 equality challenge using a rational-basis and non-arbitrariness test, and both are sufficient conditions for a challenge failing, so they do not yield contradictory outcomes.

question_a: When a rent-control or tenancy law is enacted, amended, repealed or expires, does its protection (or the withdrawal of protection) apply to eviction proceedings, tenancies or defaults that predate it or are pending when it takes effect, or is the matter governed by the earlier or general law?
question_b: Can a protected tenant be evicted, or possession decreed against them, other than through the forum and procedure laid down by the rent-control or tenancy statute and on a statutory ground that the court has found, or has material to find, established?
note: Rule A asks whether a change in tenancy law applies to earlier or pending tenancies and proceedings (temporal scope), while Rule B asks, once an occupant is protected, whether eviction must go through the statutory forum and ground; Rule B's 'protected occupant' premise is what Rule A helps determine, so the two do not yield opposing outcomes.

question_a: Must a conviction for an offence founded on group or constructive liability (common intention or unlawful assembly), or on an individual attributed act, be set aside where the evidence does not reliably prove the accused's own participation, shared intention or common object, or where the facts negate the offence, for instance private defence or no death caused?
question_b: Is an accused entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt (so that an acquittal is upheld or restored, or a conviction set aside) where the prosecution's evidence of that accused's participation in the charged offence is unreliable, contradictory, uncorroborated or in conflict with medical, ballistic or recovery evidence?
note: Both rules apply the same principle: where reliable evidence of the accused's own participation is missing and nothing else independently proves guilt, reasonable doubt operates and the conviction is set aside (or the acquittal stands), so they give consistent outcomes and can be merged, even though A adds group-liability, private-defence and missing-ingredient limbs and B adds acquittal appeals and specific evidentiary triggers.

question_a: When is a tenant's unauthorised subletting or parting with possession established for rent-control eviction: what must the landlord prove, when may exclusive possession and consideration be inferred, and when does another person's use or presence in the premises fall short because the tenant retains legal possession and control?
question_b: Is a tenant (or a person claiming through the tenant) who was let into possession by, or has attorned to, a landlord barred from denying that landlord's title, or from setting up adverse possession against it, while the tenancy continues and possession has not been surrendered?
note: Rule A asks what a landlord must prove to establish unauthorised subletting or parting with possession as a ground for eviction, while Rule B asks whether a tenant who attorned to a landlord is estopped from denying that landlord's title or claiming adverse possession, so the two rules address distinct questions and neither's conditions or outcomes contradict the other.

question_a: When does a landlord seeking eviction from rented premises for own or family occupation or business use establish a genuine (bona fide) requirement, and what must the landlord prove, including the absence of other suitable accommodation and the link between the claimed user and the landlord's own use?
question_b: When a landlord or authority proceeds for eviction on a particular statutory ground or under a special statutory procedure, is it excused from satisfying a further prerequisite or protection (such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of title, a rehousing duty or tenant-protection law) because that requirement is not part of the invoked ground or is displaced by the invoked scheme?
note: Rule A defines what a landlord must prove to establish the personal-need (bona fide requirement) ground, while Rule B asks whether extra requirements from outside the invoked ground or scheme can be imposed, so they address separate questions and do not produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: Is a civil court's jurisdiction (or a later civil suit) barred by a special tenancy, revenue, rent-control or similar statute or forum, or by that forum's earlier decision, where the forum was not empowered to decide the matter or grant the relief claimed?
question_b: Does a statutory bar on civil suits, or a special eviction or summary-eviction mechanism, oust the civil court's jurisdiction over an eviction or possession suit (or a title claim) when the special forum or bar does not cover the claim or the defendant in the suit?
note: Rule B is a narrower application of Rule A's principle that civil courts keep general jurisdiction unless a statute or competent special forum ousts it, limited to possession or title suits over immovable property where the bar or forum does not cover the claim or defendant, so the two give consistent outcomes.

question_a: When is a tenant's unauthorised subletting or parting with possession established for rent-control eviction: what must the landlord prove, when may exclusive possession and consideration be inferred, and when does another person's use or presence in the premises fall short because the tenant retains legal possession and control?
question_b: When does a tenant's denial or challenge of the landlord's title (or of the tenancy) in a rent-control eviction proceeding furnish a ground for eviction, and how far may the rent-control forum inquire into the denial without finally deciding title?
note: Rule A asks when subletting or parting with possession is proved as an eviction ground, while Rule B asks when a tenant's denial of the landlord's title is an eviction ground; these are separate statutory grounds with distinct elements and no overlapping fact pattern that would produce inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: When does an amendment apply to proceedings that were pending when it took effect, or to claims and events that arose before it, rather than operating only prospectively?
question_b: Does an amendment that alters substantive rights, or that enlarges jurisdiction over or removes the finality of an existing decision, apply to proceedings already pending or decided before it took effect when it does not expressly or by necessary implication say so?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent application of Rule A's general approach: for amendments affecting substantive rights or finality, the presumption is prospective unless retroactivity is express or necessarily implied, and a mere 'declaratory' or 'beneficial' label does not trigger Rule A's clarificatory exception where the earlier text was clear.

question_a: When a claimant seeks higher compensation for compulsorily acquired land, must the claimant prove with admissible, comparable evidence that the award is inadequate, and is enhancement refused where that proof is missing?
question_b: Under the land acquisition statutes (principally Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894), can a landowner who did not obtain an effective reference under Section 18 seek redetermination of compensation on the strength of a higher court award to another owner under the same notification, even if the owner's reference application was dismissed as time-barred or the owner accepted compensation without protest?
note: Rule A concerns the claimant's evidentiary burden to prove inadequacy in an enhancement claim, while Rule B concerns only threshold eligibility to seek Section 28-A redetermination based on another owner's higher award, so they do not yield inconsistent outcomes on the same question.

question_a: Is a tenant sued for eviction on the ground of rent default protected from eviction when the tenant has not made the payment, tender or deposit that the rent-control statute requires, in the manner and at the time it requires?
question_b: Does a tenant who has lost, or failed to preserve, the status or step on which a statutory tenant-based right depends (holding the tenancy through the decree for pre-emption, or delivering possession by the decreed date for reoccupation) lose entitlement to the statutory remedy?
note: Rule A asks whether a tenant is protected from eviction for rent default without timely payment, tender or deposit, while Rule B asks whether a tenant loses a pre-emption or reoccupation remedy by losing tenancy status or missing a stipulated step, so they address different questions and their conditions never produce opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Can a person in actual or settled possession of property obtain protection (injunction, restoration, or defence) against forcible or extra-legal dispossession, without proving title, so that anyone claiming a better right must recover possession through due process of law?
question_b: When is a suit or claim for possession not barred by limitation, given that it was filed within the prescribed period counted from dispossession, redemption or the date the defendant's possession began, including after amendment or after an earlier decree became unexecutable?
note: Rule A concerns protection of settled possession against forcible or non-judicial dispossession without proving title, whereas Rule B concerns whether a possession suit is time-barred; the two address separate questions and can operate together without producing inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: Is a compulsory acquisition that was made for a public purpose invalidated by a collateral, prior, subsequent or extraneous circumstance, such as a later diversion or release of the land, an earlier abandoned or alternative proceeding, the owner's existing or intended use, a plan or land-use mismatch, a failed negotiation, or a procedural or record irregularity, when no defect in the statutory acquisition process or the public purpose itself is shown?
question_b: Does delay or an interval in the steps of a land acquisition (between the preliminary notification, its publication or local notice, the declaration and its publication, or the completion of proceedings) invalidate the acquisition, absent proof that the statutory deadline was missed for the act the statute actually regulates or evidence of bad faith?
note: Rule A asks whether collateral or extraneous circumstances (later diversion, abandoned proceedings, owner's use, plan mismatches) invalidate an acquisition, while Rule B asks whether delay between the statutory steps of the acquisition itself does, so they address different questions, though both lean toward upholding the acquisition absent a statutory defect or bad faith.

question_a: Can a court decline discretionary writ relief against a land acquisition, or a similar public project or approval, because the challenge was brought after substantial and unexplained delay, particularly where the state has acted on the acquisition, third-party rights have arisen or the public would be prejudiced?
question_b: Where a land acquisition authority has delayed unreasonably, whether in making awards, completing the acquisition or appointing an arbitrator, should the court quash the acquisition, or preserve it and grant additional or equitable monetary relief (additional compensation, solatium or interest) to the affected owners?
note: Rule A asks whether a challenger's own unexplained delay justifies refusing discretionary writ relief, while Rule B asks what remedy applies when the acquiring authority delays, and although both tend to leave the acquisition intact, they address different questions with no conflicting outcomes.

question_a: Can a writ or public interest petition be dismissed or relief refused on the ground of delay and laches where the challenge is brought after substantial, unexplained delay, particularly after the impugned action has become final (for example, award made, possession taken, refund accepted)?
question_b: Will the Supreme Court, on appeal, interfere with or accept a procedural-timeliness or alternative-remedy objection (delay, laches, or an available statutory remedy) where the court or authority below exercised its discretion to entertain the proceeding and the objection was not pressed or the delay was explained?
note: Both rules treat delay as a matter of judicial discretion: Rule A says a writ court may refuse relief for unexplained delay, and Rule B is the narrower appellate case where the Supreme Court will not disturb a forum's decision to entertain the proceeding, so the two can both hold at once.

question_a: Can a party raise in the Supreme Court (or a higher court in the hierarchy) a plea, contention or objection that was not raised, pleaded, pursued or tried in the courts below, or was abandoned there?
question_b: Can a party obtain, at the appellate or later stage, relief, a finding or a remand that depends on a claim that was never pleaded or relief that was never sought, or on evidence that was available but not adduced below, when no recognised ground (amendment, prevention despite due diligence, or need for the court to pronounce judgment) is shown?
note: Rule A governs whether a new contention, plea or objection can be raised for the first time in a higher court, while Rule B governs whether unpleaded relief or evidence not adduced below can support a decision, finding or remand; they overlap on unpleaded matters but never give inconsistent outcomes, and neither is simply a narrower case of the other.

question_a: Is a statutory power conferring executive discretion (to exempt buildings, land, persons or transactions from a regulatory scheme, or to adjust a statutory limit) an excessive delegation or a violation of Article 14, where the provision itself lacks detailed criteria but the enactment's policy supplies guidance?
question_b: Does a rent-control (or similar) exemption or classification that treats a defined class of buildings, owners or tenants differently satisfy Article 14 where it rests on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the purpose of the legislation?
note: Rule A asks whether conferring executive discretion to exempt or relax a regulatory scheme is excessive delegation or arbitrary under Article 14, while Rule B asks whether the legislature's own classification or exemption has an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the statute's purpose, so they test different things and can both be satisfied without conflict.

question_a: When will an appellate court, especially the Supreme Court, decline to disturb a lower court's or tribunal's valuation or compensation award for acquired land or property, and when will it intervene?
question_b: When may an appellate, revisional or supervisory court (including the Supreme Court under Article 136) interfere with a lower court's discretionary decision, and when must it leave that decision undisturbed?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B's general deference principle to valuation and compensation awards, and its conditions (no error of principle, no overlooked or misapplied evidence) fit within Rule B's grounds for interference, so the two give consistent outcomes.

question_a: Can a party raise in an appeal (including an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court) a ground, contention or objection that it did not raise, plead, pursue or preserve in the courts below?
question_b: When a party who won below (or who did not appeal) is respondent in an appeal, may it support the decree on grounds or findings decided against it without filing its own appeal or cross-objection, and when must it appeal or cross-object?
note: Rule A asks whether a ground not raised or preserved below can be taken for the first time on appeal, while Rule B asks whether a respondent holding a favourable decree needs its own appeal or cross-objection to defend that decree on grounds decided against it, so the two can apply together without producing opposite outcomes.

question_a: When compensation for compulsorily acquired land is awarded or enhanced by a court, does it carry the statutory additions (solatium, additional amount and interest), and does the interest payable on compensation extend to the solatium and other additions?
question_b: When a court enhances or redetermines compensation for acquired or requisitioned property, does interest run on that compensation from the date possession was taken until payment, and may it be withheld for a period of delay in appealing?
note: Both rules concern interest on enhanced compensation for acquired land. Rule A states the general entitlement, including interest on solatium, and Rule B restates it for acquired or requisitioned property and adds a recognised exception for periods of appeal delay, which Rule A does not contradict.

question_a: When may a court condone delay in applying to substitute the legal representatives of a deceased party (and set aside abatement) in a pending appeal or proceeding, and what must the applicant show for the delay to be condoned?
question_b: When may a court or authority condone a delay (or a failure to meet a procedural time limit) in filing a proceeding, and on what showing of sufficient cause, such as bona fide pursuit of another remedy or an explained delay?
note: Rule A applies the general power to condone delay in Rule B to the specific setting of substituting legal representatives and setting aside abatement, and it is consistent with Rule B because 'sufficient cause' already implies the absence of negligence or mala fides.

question_a: When a competent legislature retrospectively validates earlier acts (acquisitions, vestings, evictions) that were defective or made under a repealed or invalid law, does the validation sustain those acts against challenges based on the cured defect, such as a missing procedural step, a prior court order, a repealed law, or discrimination between procedures?
question_b: Does a law or grant condition that restricts, regulates or retrospectively affects property rights (by limiting transfers, evictions, rents or recovery of possession) infringe the constitutional property guarantees (Articles 19(1)(f), 31, 31A) when it is a reasonable measure serving a public purpose, or when the claimant's interest was defeasible or merely regulated rather than acquired?
note: Rule A asks whether retrospective validation cures a defect in earlier acts, while Rule B asks whether a property restriction or defeasible interest infringes Articles 19(1)(f), 31 and 31A; they are consistent and could apply together (B can help decide whether a validating law has an 'independent constitutional violation' under A), but they do not address the same question.

question_a: When is a compulsory land acquisition, or an action built on it, invalid because the power was used for an extraneous or private purpose, or because the notification or procedure did not meet the statutory requirements for the stated purpose?
question_b: When is a law or custom that restricts or deprives a person of property invalid because the restriction is not reasonable and in the interests of the general public, or because the deprivation lacks a public purpose?
note: Rule A tests whether an executive acquisition or notification under a valid statute was used for an extraneous purpose or failed statutory requirements, while Rule B tests whether a law or custom is constitutionally invalid for lacking public purpose or reasonableness, so they address different questions even though both involve public purpose and give no contradictory outcomes.

question_a: When a court enhances or redetermines compensation for acquired or requisitioned property, does interest run on that compensation from the date possession was taken until payment, and may it be withheld for a period of delay in appealing?
question_b: Where interest is paid or claimed in connection with compensation for compulsorily acquired land or withheld money, how is that interest characterised as distinct from the compensation itself, both for tax purposes (revenue receipt or capital) and for the base on which it is computed?
note: Rule A asks whether and from when interest runs on enhanced or unpaid acquisition compensation (and when it may be excluded for appeal delay), while Rule B asks how such interest is characterised, as a taxable revenue receipt separate from compensation, so both can hold together without producing different outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Does a landlord's acceptance of rent or equivalent payments after a lease or tenancy has expired or been terminated create a new tenancy by holding over, or waive a termination notice or eviction ground, in the absence of the landlord's clear assent to continued possession or intention to treat the lease as subsisting?
question_b: Is a tenant (or a person claiming through the tenant) who was let into possession by, or has attorned to, a landlord barred from denying that landlord's title, or from setting up adverse possession against it, while the tenancy continues and possession has not been surrendered?
note: Rule A asks whether a landlord's acceptance of rent after a tenancy ends creates a new tenancy or waives a notice or eviction ground, while Rule B asks whether a tenant whose tenancy continues can deny the landlord's title or claim adverse possession, so the questions and outcomes do not overlap and no facts would produce contradictory results.

question_a: When a tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears in the manner or within the time the statute, the court or the landlord's accepted practice allows, can the landlord still obtain eviction for rent default?
question_b: When a landlord seeks eviction for rent default under a state rent-control statute, what must a tenant pay or tender, when, and how regularly, to obtain or keep the statutory protection from eviction, and what happens if the tenant falls short?
note: Both rules ask when a tenant escapes rent-default eviction by paying, but Rule A protects a tenant who pays or tenders in a manner the court allows or the landlord has long accepted without protest, while Rule B denies protection for any irregular or late payment and says courts have no discretion, so the two diverge on facts like irregular payments the landlord accepted; because their date ranges overlap, the difference is better explained by unstated differences in statutory scheme (for example, statutes with mandatory deposit-and-continue-paying conditions versus those allowing cure or court discretion) than by a doctrinal shift.

question_a: When a landlord seeks eviction under a rent-control statute on a ground such as bona fide requirement, rebuilding or demolition, or change of use, must the landlord plead and prove that ground on evidence, with the need assessed objectively on all surrounding circumstances rather than on mere desire or bare assertion?
question_b: In a summary eviction proceeding where the tenant must obtain leave to contest or defend, when must the Controller or court grant leave, and when may it refuse leave?
note: Rule A concerns the landlord's burden to plead and prove a statutory ground at the merits stage, while Rule B concerns when a tenant must be granted leave to contest at the preliminary stage of summary eviction, so the two address different questions and can apply together without any outcome clash.

question_a: When the law changes while an appeal or other proceeding is pending, must the appellate court decide it under the changed law, or does the earlier law (or a vested right) continue to govern?
question_b: When a tenancy or rent-control enactment, amendment or extension takes effect while an eviction or possession proceeding (suit, appeal or revision) is pending, does the changed law govern that pending proceeding?
note: Rule B is a narrower application of Rule A's general principle to rent-control and tenancy changes during pending eviction or possession proceedings, with the same conditions (express or necessary-implication retroactivity, appeal as continuation of the suit, no saving provision) and consistent outcomes.

question_a: Once possession of land has been taken under an acquisition (or the statutory vesting event has occurred) and the land has vested absolutely in the State free from encumbrances, can that vesting be undone by withdrawal, release, lapse for delayed award, later legislation or later orders, or by the former owner's claim to restoration?
question_b: Is a compulsory acquisition that was made for a public purpose invalidated by a collateral, prior, subsequent or extraneous circumstance, such as a later diversion or release of the land, an earlier abandoned or alternative proceeding, the owner's existing or intended use, a plan or land-use mismatch, a failed negotiation, or a procedural or record irregularity, when no defect in the statutory acquisition process or the public purpose itself is shown?
note: Rule A asks whether a completed vesting after possession can be reversed by withdrawal, lapse, later law or a restoration claim, while Rule B asks whether the acquisition's validity is undermined by collateral or extraneous circumstances. The two overlap on later release or diversion but are consistent and neither is a subset of the other.

question_a: When is a tenant's unauthorised subletting or parting with possession established for rent-control eviction: what must the landlord prove, when may exclusive possession and consideration be inferred, and when does another person's use or presence in the premises fall short because the tenant retains legal possession and control?
question_b: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
note: Rule A decides whether a tenant's subletting or parting with possession is established as an eviction ground, while Rule B decides whether a separate notice terminating the tenancy is needed before eviction, so the two address distinct legal questions that do not yield conflicting outcomes on any set of facts.

question_a: When a party who won below (or who did not appeal) is respondent in an appeal, may it support the decree on grounds or findings decided against it without filing its own appeal or cross-objection, and when must it appeal or cross-object?
question_b: When, and within what limits, may an appellate court under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC grant relief to, or vary a decree in favour of, a party who did not appeal or file cross-objections?
note: Rule A sets the general position (a respondent may defend its decree without a cross-objection, but needs its own appeal or cross-objection to alter the decree or get greater relief), and Rule B is a cautious, court-driven exception (Order 41 Rule 33) that lets the appellate court grant relief to a non-appealing party who is before it, to do complete justice or avoid inconsistent decrees, without overriding legal bars or reopening finalized independent parts.

question_a: Is an acquisition law, or an acquisition made under it, unconstitutional or invalid merely because it omits compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation that another scheme provides or that the challenger says is required?
question_b: Can solatium (and interest) be denied to owners of compulsorily acquired land merely because the land is acquired under a special or different enactment, for a different public purpose or by a different authority, rather than under the general land-acquisition law?
note: Both rules ask whether omitting solatium or interest invalidates an acquisition law, and on facts where a law is protected by a constitutional shield (such as Article 31A, 31C or the Ninth Schedule) or involves a distinct statutory scheme, Rule A upholds the omission while Rule B would strike it down under Article 14 for lack of a rational basis, so the difference is best explained by that unstated shield or statutory-scheme distinction.

question_a: Does a statutory or policy classification that treats a defined class of persons, property, institutions or transactions differently violate the Article 14 guarantee of equality when it rests on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the object of the law?
question_b: Is a special or summary statutory procedure affecting tenants' or occupants' possession and property rights (eviction, clearance or redevelopment) constitutionally valid under Articles 14 and 19 where it rests on a reasonable classification or public purpose and gives affected persons notice, an opportunity to object or defend, and review or appeal safeguards?
note: Rule B applies the Article 14 reasonable-classification test of Rule A to special or summary possession procedures (eviction, clearance, redevelopment), adding Article 19 and procedural-safeguard conditions, and the two rules never produce opposite outcomes.

question_a: Does eyewitness testimony in a criminal case have to be rejected because of minor or collateral discrepancies, omissions in the first report, delay, relationship of the witnesses, absence of independent or forensic corroboration, or medical evidence that does not wholly exclude the account?
question_b: What is the effect of the prosecution's failure to explain injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence: does it require rejection of, or reasonable doubt about, the prosecution case, or can the case stand where the injuries are minor or the prosecution evidence is clear, cogent and credible?
note: Rule A concerns whether credible eyewitness testimony can be rejected for minor discrepancies, delay, relationship or missing corroboration, while Rule B concerns the effect of the prosecution's failure to explain an accused's injuries; they address distinct questions and can be applied together without contradiction.

question_a: Does a land-related law, tax, compensation scheme or State action in acquisition, release or withdrawal violate the equality guarantee of Article 14 when it treats similarly situated persons or properties differently (or dissimilar ones alike) without an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object of the law?
question_b: Does a law that singles out particular persons or a group for a disability or adverse treatment, while leaving comparable persons unaffected and without any rational basis or substantial distinguishing attribute, violate the equal protection guarantee of Article 14 and become void under Article 13?
note: Rule A applies the Article 14 reasonable-classification test, which Rule B states generally for laws singling out persons for adverse treatment, to the land context (acquisition, release, withdrawal, tax and compensation); it also adds executive action and the dissimilar-treated-alike limb, and the two never yield different outcomes.

question_a: Is a compulsory acquisition that was made for a public purpose invalidated by a collateral, prior, subsequent or extraneous circumstance, such as a later diversion or release of the land, an earlier abandoned or alternative proceeding, the owner's existing or intended use, a plan or land-use mismatch, a failed negotiation, or a procedural or record irregularity, when no defect in the statutory acquisition process or the public purpose itself is shown?
question_b: Is a special acquisition, town-planning or improvement scheme invalid under the equality guarantee (Article 14) merely because its procedure, compensation method or review mechanism differs from the general land-acquisition law, or because another acquisition law could theoretically be used?
note: Rule A asks whether collateral, prior, subsequent or extraneous circumstances invalidate an otherwise valid public-purpose acquisition, while Rule B asks whether a special acquisition or planning scheme violates Article 14 merely because it departs from the general acquisition law, so the two rules address different legal questions and would not yield opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Is a compulsory acquisition that was made for a public purpose invalidated by a collateral, prior, subsequent or extraneous circumstance, such as a later diversion or release of the land, an earlier abandoned or alternative proceeding, the owner's existing or intended use, a plan or land-use mismatch, a failed negotiation, or a procedural or record irregularity, when no defect in the statutory acquisition process or the public purpose itself is shown?
question_b: When an acquisition is governed by a special, self-contained statute (or a special scheme that declares itself exclusive), can provisions of the general land-acquisition law (time limits, lapse, procedures, redetermination, or the general acquisition power itself) be applied to it?
note: Rule A asks whether collateral or extraneous circumstances invalidate an otherwise valid public-purpose acquisition, while Rule B asks whether general land-acquisition law provisions apply to acquisitions under a special self-contained statute, so the questions are distinct and their outcomes do not contradict each other.

question_a: When material facts or title are seriously disputed, or the claim is purely contractual or private-law, should a court exercising writ jurisdiction under Article 226 (or 32) decline to decide the dispute and leave the claimant to a civil remedy, and when may it still decide?
question_b: Can a High Court use its writ (Article 226) or supervisory (Article 227) jurisdiction to adjudicate a property, possession or landlord-tenant dispute between private parties when no breach of a public or statutory duty by a public authority is alleged and ordinary civil remedies are available?
note: Rule B is a narrower application of Rule A's principle to private property, possession and tenancy disputes between private parties, adding Article 227 and the exceptions of public-duty breach, state collusion and jurisdictional excess, and neither rule requires a writ court to decide a dispute that the other tells it to leave to civil remedies.

question_a: Does a statutory or policy classification that treats a defined class of persons, property, institutions or transactions differently violate the Article 14 guarantee of equality when it rests on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the object of the law?
question_b: Does a rent-control (or similar) exemption or classification that treats a defined class of buildings, owners or tenants differently satisfy Article 14 where it rests on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the purpose of the legislation?
note: Rule B applies the general Article 14 reasonable-classification test in Rule A (intelligible differentia, rational nexus, not arbitrary) to the narrower setting of rent-control and trust-regulation exemptions, and the two rules always give consistent outcomes.

question_a: When an instrument that requires registration is unregistered, can it still be received or relied on for a limited or collateral purpose (such as proving a contract in a specific-performance suit, the nature of possession, or the factum of a tenancy), even though it cannot be used to prove or give effect to the transaction affecting immovable property?
question_b: Where a lease of immovable property falls within the categories that must be registered (year to year, term exceeding one year, or reserving yearly rent) and the document is unregistered, can the document be used to create the lease, prove it, or prove its terms, including as 'collateral' evidence?
note: Rule B applies the Section 49 proviso from Rule A to compulsorily registrable leases, where an unregistered lease cannot prove the lease or its terms, even under a 'collateral' label, but can still be used for truly independent purposes such as the nature of possession or the bare fact of tenancy.

question_a: Can a protected tenant be evicted, or possession decreed against them, other than through the forum and procedure laid down by the rent-control or tenancy statute and on a statutory ground that the court has found, or has material to find, established?
question_b: Where a statute provides a specific remedy or procedure for a claimed right (adjustment or refund of excess rent, or restoration of possession to a tenant), can the party bypass it by relying on an automatic or general-law set-off, or on a summary procedure?
note: Rule A asks whether a protected tenant can be evicted outside the statutory forum and without a statutory ground, while Rule B asks whether a party can bypass a specific statutory remedy (excess-rent adjustment or restoration) through set-off or a summary procedure; both reflect the principle that statutory procedures are exclusive, but they address different questions and never yield opposite outcomes.

question_a: Under rent-control legislation, when does a tenant's act (subletting without the required consent, use contrary to the lease, or construction or alteration of the premises) establish a statutory ground for eviction, and what must the landlord prove?
question_b: Can a protected tenant be evicted, or possession decreed against them, other than through the forum and procedure laid down by the rent-control or tenancy statute and on a statutory ground that the court has found, or has material to find, established?
note: Rule A states when specific tenant acts (subletting, misuse, construction) establish a statutory eviction ground and what the landlord must prove, while Rule B states that eviction of a protected occupant needs the proper statutory forum and procedure and an established ground, so the two address different questions and are complementary, with no conflicting outcomes.

question_a: Must a court or authority give a person notice and a fair opportunity to be heard, including disclosure of adverse material, before making an order that prejudicially affects that person's rights or civil interests, and what follows if it does not?
question_b: Must a person who is not the direct party to an administrative or statutory proceeding, but whose interests (possessory, tenancy, beneficiary or bidder interests) may be adversely affected by its outcome, be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the decision is made?
note: Rule B is a narrower application of Rule A's general audi alteram partem principle to non-party persons with a cognisable interest (tenant, beneficiary, bidder) in administrative or statutory proceedings, with the same exclusion-by-law exception and the same consequence (order vitiated and decision redone after hearing), so the two are consistent.

question_a: Under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, can an execution sale be set aside for material irregularity or fraud in its publication or conduct, and is proof that the irregularity caused substantial injury to the applicant required?
question_b: When an execution court's sale of property is challenged for non-compliance with the Order XXI CPC procedure (proclamation, notice, deposit, conduct of auction), is the sale void as a nullity or voidable for material irregularity or inadequacy, and what must the court do to avoid setting it aside?
note: Rule A governs Order XXI Rule 90 challenges to sales with material irregularity or fraud, where substantial injury must be proved, while Rule B carves out a narrower category of sales that breach mandatory Order XXI requirements or lack judicial application of mind, which are treated as nullities outside Rule 90 and so need no injury showing.

question_a: When an instrument that requires registration is unregistered, can it still be received or relied on for a limited or collateral purpose (such as proving a contract in a specific-performance suit, the nature of possession, or the factum of a tenancy), even though it cannot be used to prove or give effect to the transaction affecting immovable property?
question_b: Where a transfer of immovable property must be made by a registered instrument, can an oral sale, an agreement or contract to sell, an unregistered document, or delivery of possession alone transfer title or create an interest in the property before a registered conveyance is completed?
note: Rule A concerns whether an unregistered instrument is admissible as evidence for a collateral purpose, while Rule B concerns whether title or an interest in the property passes without a registered conveyance; the two are complementary and consistent, since a contract to sell can be proved for specific performance without transferring title.

question_a: Does a limited or restricted interest held by a Hindu woman in property that she possessed when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 commenced, and that rests on a pre-existing right such as maintenance, become absolute ownership under Section 14(1) rather than remaining restricted under Section 14(2)?
question_b: When a Hindu woman holds property under a will or other instrument that expressly gives her only a restricted (for example lifetime) interest, does Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 enlarge that interest into absolute ownership, or does the Section 14(2) exception keep it restricted?
note: Both rules apply the same Section 14(1)/14(2) test (a pre-existing right leads to enlargement, a new restricted grant does not), and Rule B is the narrower Section 14(2) exception for restricted grants under a will or instrument, so the two are consistent.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: Does a law or grant condition that restricts, regulates or retrospectively affects property rights (by limiting transfers, evictions, rents or recovery of possession) infringe the constitutional property guarantees (Articles 19(1)(f), 31, 31A) when it is a reasonable measure serving a public purpose, or when the claimant's interest was defeasible or merely regulated rather than acquired?
note: Rule A asks whether Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B give a law immunity from Part III challenge, whether or not the law is reasonable, while Rule B asks whether a regulatory or restrictive measure infringes property rights on the merits (reasonableness, public interest, defeasible interest); both end in 'challenge fails' but through separate tests, so they never produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: What must the statutory objection-and-hearing procedure before a compulsory land acquisition (chiefly Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894) provide, and what follows when the procedure is or is not complied with?
question_b: Must a person who is not the direct party to an administrative or statutory proceeding, but whose interests (possessory, tenancy, beneficiary or bidder interests) may be adversely affected by its outcome, be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the decision is made?
note: Rule A asks what a statutory objection hearing must contain (a genuine hearing and real consideration) for objectors in land acquisition, while Rule B asks whether non-party interested persons are entitled to notice and a hearing at all, so they address different questions and are consistent on overlapping facts.

question_a: When may a High Court, in second appeal (or analogous revision), interfere with or reappraise the factual findings of the lower courts, including concurrent findings, and when must it leave them undisturbed?
question_b: When may or should an appellate court remand a matter to the court below for determination, and when must it instead decide the appeal itself on the existing record?
note: Rule A addresses when a High Court in second appeal may disturb lower courts' factual findings, while Rule B addresses when an appellate court should remand rather than decide the appeal itself, so they are separate questions and do not give inconsistent outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Must a first appellate court (or other appellate authority) deciding an appeal on fact and law independently assess the evidence, decide the material issues, and give reasons, engaging with the trial court's reasoning where it reverses, and what is the consequence of failing to do so?
question_b: When may an appellate, revisional or supervisory court (including the Supreme Court under Article 136) interfere with a lower court's discretionary decision, and when must it leave that decision undisturbed?
note: Rule A sets the duties of a first appellate court deciding on fact and law (independent assessment, reasons, and the consequence of failing to give them), while Rule B sets the limited standard on which a higher court reviews a lower court's discretionary order, so they address different questions and give no inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: Where premises are let for both residential and non-residential (professional or business) purposes, or a residential letting is openly used for non-residential purposes with the landlord's consent, can the landlord evict on a ground that depends on the premises being residential (landlord's residential need, or tenant's acquisition of other residence)?
question_b: Does a tenant's departure from the specific use for which premises were let (an additional or different trade, incidental residential or resting use, a different occupant, or a business in part of a residential building) amount to use for a different purpose that justifies eviction, where the general character of the letting is preserved and the landlord's interest is not prejudiced?
note: Rule A asks whether residence-based eviction grounds (landlord's residential need, tenant's acquisition of other residence) are available for mixed or consented non-residential tenancies, while Rule B asks whether a departure from the specified use amounts to a change of user ground, so they concern different eviction grounds and cannot yield conflicting outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Is a tenant sued for eviction on the ground of rent default protected from eviction when the tenant has not made the payment, tender or deposit that the rent-control statute requires, in the manner and at the time it requires?
question_b: When a tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears in the manner or within the time the statute, the court or the landlord's accepted practice allows, can the landlord still obtain eviction for rent default?
note: The rules are mostly converse (A: strict non-compliance leaves the tenant evictable; B: permitted cure or payment bars eviction), but they clash where the tenant paid irregularly, outside the statutory manner or time, and the landlord long accepted it without protest, since A says no protection and B says not evictable. The split is best explained by an unstated statutory difference: whether the statute makes timely statutory payment mandatory and non-curable, or requires wilful or habitual default and gives the court or landlord room to excuse or accept cure.

question_a: Can a final land-acquisition compensation award or decree be reopened, whether by redetermination or by a later application for additional statutory benefits, when the applicant has no statutory basis for doing so, such as a prior reference, a missed limitation period, or a request beyond mere correction?
question_b: Can a court (reference court or civil court) determine or enhance compensation for acquired land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when no valid reference on compensation has been made to it under Section 18, and can that defect be cured by acquiescence, a later clarification, or an ordinary suit?
note: Rule A asks whether a final award or decree can be reopened outside the Act's express remedies, while Rule B asks whether a court has jurisdiction over compensation without a valid Section 18 reference; both confine compensation proceedings to statutory routes and never give opposing outcomes.

question_a: Is a land-reform or agrarian-reform law (including acquisition of estates, land-ceiling laws, tenant-ownership laws and amendments to them) immune from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31 (or Part III generally) by virtue of Article 31A, Article 31B/Ninth Schedule or related provisions, and what conditions must be met for that immunity, such as presidential assent for a State law?
question_b: When is a constitutional challenge to a land acquisition, requisition or land-reform law (on grounds such as violation of property rights, colourable legislation, absence of public purpose, or confiscatory deprivation) rejected?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B's 'express constitutional saving' limb (Articles 31A/31B and the Ninth Schedule for agrarian-reform laws) and bars only fundamental-rights challenges, so it does not contradict Rule B's broader competence-based test.

question_a: Can a claimant obtain declaratory, injunctive, possessory or other property-related relief when the claimant has not established the foundational right on which the relief depends, such as title, actual or lawful possession, a lawful interest, or a legal status?
question_b: When does a limitation provision that is tied to the plaintiff's dispossession or prior possession (such as Art. 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908 or an analogous special-law provision) bar a suit for possession, and when does it not apply because the claim rests on a different basis, such as a new or reversionary title, unlawful possession, or no dispossession by the defendant?
note: Rule A asks whether property relief fails when the underlying right (title, possession, interest or status) is not proved, while Rule B asks when a dispossession-based limitation provision applies to a possession suit, so they address separate questions and do not produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: In a suit for possession of immovable property based on title under the Limitation Act, 1963 (Article 65), once the plaintiff proves title, who must prove that adverse possession has defeated it, and is the plaintiff required to prove possession within the preceding twelve years?
question_b: When does a limitation provision that is tied to the plaintiff's dispossession or prior possession (such as Art. 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908 or an analogous special-law provision) bar a suit for possession, and when does it not apply because the claim rests on a different basis, such as a new or reversionary title, unlawful possession, or no dispossession by the defendant?
note: Both rules address how limitation operates in possession suits, but where the plaintiff proves title and not possession within twelve years, Rule B's Art. 142-type provision bars the suit while Rule A's Art. 65 (1963 Act) does not, a difference that comes from the change in statutory regime (the 1908 Act's dispossession-based provision versus the 1963 Act's adverse-possession-based provision) rather than from any real disagreement in the courts' reasoning.

question_a: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
question_b: Is a tenant (or a person claiming through the tenant) who was let into possession by, or has attorned to, a landlord barred from denying that landlord's title, or from setting up adverse possession against it, while the tenancy continues and possession has not been surrendered?
note: Rule A asks when a separate notice terminating the tenancy is needed before eviction, while Rule B asks whether a tenant who attorned to a landlord is estopped from denying the landlord's title or claiming adverse possession; they share a landlord-tenant setting but answer different legal questions and cannot yield contradictory outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: When a rent-control or tenancy law is enacted, amended, repealed or expires, does its protection (or the withdrawal of protection) apply to eviction proceedings, tenancies or defaults that predate it or are pending when it takes effect, or is the matter governed by the earlier or general law?
question_b: When rent-control protection is extended to, or withdrawn from, premises (or an exemption period expires) while an eviction proceeding is pending, is the proceeding governed by the law in force when it was instituted, or does the later change apply to it?
note: Rule B applies Rule A's presumption of prospectivity to the narrower case of eviction proceedings pending when rent-control coverage changes, and both give the same outcome (the law at institution governs) unless the legislature provides otherwise.

question_a: Is a state law that acquires or vests land, minerals or an undertaking invalid for want of legislative competence or for repugnancy to a central law on a related subject (planning, mining, forests, industry control, electricity or land acquisition), where the two laws have different dominant purposes and can operate together?
question_b: What is the effect of presidential assent (or the absence or limited scope of assent) on the validity and enforceability of a State law that is challenged as repugnant to central law or as infringing the property provisions of Article 31?
note: Rule A asks whether a state law is repugnant or beyond competence in the first place (no irreconcilable conflict, different field), while Rule B asks whether presidential assent saves or limits a state law, so they are complementary and never give opposite outcomes.

question_a: What is the effect of the prosecution's failure to explain injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence: does it require rejection of, or reasonable doubt about, the prosecution case, or can the case stand where the injuries are minor or the prosecution evidence is clear, cogent and credible?
question_b: Is an accused entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt (so that an acquittal is upheld or restored, or a conviction set aside) where the prosecution's evidence of that accused's participation in the charged offence is unreliable, contradictory, uncorroborated or in conflict with medical, ballistic or recovery evidence?
note: Rule A asks whether unexplained injuries to the accused alone defeat the prosecution case, while Rule B asks whether unreliable or uncorroborated evidence of an accused's participation leaves reasonable doubt; they address distinct issues and give no contradictory outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Can a protected tenant be evicted, or possession decreed against them, other than through the forum and procedure laid down by the rent-control or tenancy statute and on a statutory ground that the court has found, or has material to find, established?
question_b: When rent-control protection is extended to, or withdrawn from, premises (or an exemption period expires) while an eviction proceeding is pending, is the proceeding governed by the law in force when it was instituted, or does the later change apply to it?
note: Rule A bars eviction of a protected occupant outside the statutory forum and grounds, while Rule B lets a proceeding validly instituted before protection began continue under the law at institution. On facts where protection is extended mid-suit, they give opposite outcomes. The unstated fact that reconciles them is whether the occupant was protected at institution or only became protected during pendency, together with any legislative provision for pending cases.

question_a: In an eviction proceeding founded on rent default, does the outcome depend on whether the tenant followed the payment, deposit or demand procedure prescribed by the rent statute, and is the consequence of non-compliance limited to what the statute provides rather than being automatic eviction?
question_b: Where a statute provides a specific remedy or procedure for a claimed right (adjustment or refund of excess rent, or restoration of possession to a tenant), can the party bypass it by relying on an automatic or general-law set-off, or on a summary procedure?
note: Rule A asks what consequence follows when a tenant fails to follow a statutory payment, deposit or demand procedure (only the statutory consequence, not automatic eviction), while Rule B asks whether a party can bypass a statutory remedy through set-off or a summary procedure (no); the two share a theme of statutory exclusivity but address different questions, and they never produce opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: When may or should an appellate court remand a matter to the court below for determination, and when must it instead decide the appeal itself on the existing record?
question_b: When a lower court or revisional or supervisory authority has not decided a material issue on the merits, or has decided it on an incomplete or unclear footing, may the appellate court set aside the decision and remand the matter for a fresh decision?
note: Both rules address when an appellate court may remand, and they are consistent: Rule A is the general test (material issue undecided or record insufficient, and the appellate court cannot decide on the existing record), while Rule B applies it to set-aside decisions and adds specific triggers (unconsidered evidence, additional evidence needing proof or rebuttal, unclear or constraining earlier remand) with 'fresh determination necessary' roughly matching A's limiting condition.

question_a: Does an earlier proceeding that ended without a reasoned decision on the merits (a non-speaking or in limine dismissal, refusal of special leave, withdrawal, or dismissal for laches or alternative remedy) bar a later proceeding on the same matter through res judicata, merger or precedent?
question_b: Will the Supreme Court, on appeal, interfere with or accept a procedural-timeliness or alternative-remedy objection (delay, laches, or an available statutory remedy) where the court or authority below exercised its discretion to entertain the proceeding and the objection was not pressed or the delay was explained?
note: Rule A asks whether an earlier non-merits disposal (including dismissal for laches or alternative remedy) precludes a later proceeding, while Rule B asks whether the Supreme Court on appeal will accept a delay or alternative-remedy objection when the forum below exercised discretion to entertain the case, so they address separate questions and can apply together without producing opposite outcomes.

question_a: Under what conditions may an appellate court admit additional evidence (Order XLI Rule 27 CPC, Section 391 Cr.P.C., or inherent power), and what must the court do when such an application is made?
question_b: When may or should an appellate court remand a matter to the court below for determination, and when must it instead decide the appeal itself on the existing record?
note: Rule A governs when an appellate court may receive additional evidence itself, while Rule B governs when it should remand instead of deciding on the existing record; they are related procedural tools but answer different questions and do not produce inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: When may an appellate court reverse or interfere with an acquittal, and must it leave the acquittal undisturbed where the trial court's view of the evidence is reasonable or possible and the evidence permits two views?
question_b: When may the Supreme Court, hearing an appeal (typically by special leave under Article 136), disturb concurrent findings of fact reached by the trial court and the appellate or High Court?
note: Rule A governs when an appellate court may reverse an acquittal (the presumption of innocence and the 'two reasonable views' principle), while Rule B governs when the Supreme Court may disturb concurrent findings of fact under Article 136; they overlap only in an appeal against a concurrent acquittal, where both counsel deference and give the same outcome, so neither is a subset of the other and they do not conflict.

question_a: When does land acquisition for a housing scheme (including one run by a cooperative society, a joint venture, or for a limited group or workers) qualify as a 'public purpose', and what conditions (government sanction or approval, a genuine scheme, correct statutory route) must be met for it to be valid?
question_b: Is a public purpose for acquisition (or for later disposal of acquired land) valid and sufficiently specific when it is stated in general terms, such as planned development, housing or industrial and residential development, for a large area, so long as it serves the community or common good?
note: Rule A is the narrower housing-specific case, setting conditions such as a genuine approved scheme, public control and the correct statutory route, while Rule B is the broader principle that a general purpose like housing is valid and not too vague if it serves the common good, so the two are consistent.

question_a: Does a special summary eviction procedure for unauthorised occupants of public (government or municipal) premises violate the Article 14 equality guarantee because it differs from the procedure for private premises, or because an ordinary civil remedy is also available?
question_b: Does a statutory or policy classification that treats a defined class of persons, property, institutions or transactions differently violate the Article 14 guarantee of equality when it rests on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the object of the law?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B's reasonable-classification test to special summary eviction procedures for public premises, adding specific conditions (speedy recovery, safeguards, not substantially more drastic) while reaching the same outcome of no Article 14 violation.

question_a: Can a claim or relief that is already barred by limitation, whether by a fresh suit or by a belated amendment of the pleadings, be sustained or allowed to relate back, so as to defeat the opposing party's accrued limitation right?
question_b: Can a court refuse a party's belated request to add parties, amend pleadings, remand for further evidence or summon evidence when the request comes at a very late stage and the party failed to plead or join the matter earlier, or the request is unnecessary to decide the case?
note: Rule A asks whether a time-barred claim or amendment can relate back to defeat an accrued limitation right, while Rule B asks whether a court may use its discretion to refuse procedural requests made at a late stage of the proceedings, so they have different triggers (expiry of the limitation period versus lateness or unnecessariness) and are consistent where they overlap on amendments.

question_a: When should the Supreme Court set aside or commute a death sentence for murder and substitute life imprisonment, because the case is not a rarest-of-rare case and the circumstances of the crime and the offender do not show that life imprisonment is inadequate?
question_b: When may the Supreme Court set aside or commute a death sentence for murder and substitute life imprisonment, on the basis of mitigating circumstances, the offender's personal characteristics, the background to the crime, or delay and prolonged exposure to the sentence?
note: Both rules ask when the Supreme Court commutes a murder death sentence to life imprisonment because death is not the only adequate punishment, and they give consistent outcomes with overlapping triggers (mitigation, with A adding unproved aggravation and B adding non-accused-caused delay), so they can be merged.

question_a: Does a land-related law, tax, compensation scheme or State action in acquisition, release or withdrawal violate the equality guarantee of Article 14 when it treats similarly situated persons or properties differently (or dissimilar ones alike) without an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object of the law?
question_b: Does a rent-control provision that differentiates between residential and non-residential premises (in eviction grounds or in tenant protection) violate Article 14 when the distinction lacks a rational nexus to the statute's objects, including where changed circumstances have removed its original rationale?
note: Rule B applies the same Article 14 reasonable-classification test as Rule A to a narrower setting (rent-control distinctions between residential and non-residential premises), and both rules reach consistent outcomes, so B is a specific application of A's general principle.

question_a: When may or should an appellate court remand a matter to the court below for determination, and when must it instead decide the appeal itself on the existing record?
question_b: When an appellate court finds that material factual or title/possession questions in a land or property dispute remain unresolved because of an inadequate record, procedural error or erroneous reasoning below, should it remand the matter for fresh determination rather than decide it finally?
note: Rule B applies Rule A's general remand principle (material issue unresolved, record inadequate, remand not routine or futile) to land and property disputes, adding only a consent-to-retrial trigger and a futility exception, so the two are consistent and B is the narrower case.

question_a: When a landlord or authority proceeds for eviction on a particular statutory ground or under a special statutory procedure, is it excused from satisfying a further prerequisite or protection (such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of title, a rehousing duty or tenant-protection law) because that requirement is not part of the invoked ground or is displaced by the invoked scheme?
question_b: When rent-control protection is extended to, or withdrawn from, premises (or an exemption period expires) while an eviction proceeding is pending, is the proceeding governed by the law in force when it was instituted, or does the later change apply to it?
note: Rule A asks whether an additional statutory requirement or protection can be excused when eviction proceeds under an invoked ground or scheme, while Rule B asks which law governs a pending eviction proceeding when rent-control coverage changes, so the questions are distinct and the rules would not yield opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: When may an appellate court reverse or interfere with an acquittal, and must it leave the acquittal undisturbed where the trial court's view of the evidence is reasonable or possible and the evidence permits two views?
question_b: When may an appellate, revisional or supervisory court (including the Supreme Court under Article 136) interfere with a lower court's discretionary decision, and when must it leave that decision undisturbed?
note: Rule A (no interference with a reasonably possible acquittal unless perverse or unsustainable) is a narrower application of Rule B's general principle of non-interference with a reasoned discretionary decision absent arbitrariness or perversity, and the two give consistent outcomes.

question_a: When does a litigant or public authority show 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act (or an equivalent power) so that a delay in filing an appeal or similar challenge should be condoned and the matter heard on its merits?
question_b: When may an ex parte decree or ex parte dismissal be set aside, or delay in challenging it condoned, because the party was not served, did not know of the proceedings or decree, or had sufficient cause for non-appearance or delay?
note: Rule B applies the liberal 'sufficient cause' and no-gross-negligence/mala fides test of Rule A to the narrower setting of ex parte decrees and default orders (non-service, lack of knowledge, non-appearance), and the two give consistent outcomes.

question_a: When a rent-control or tenancy law is enacted, amended, repealed or expires, does its protection (or the withdrawal of protection) apply to eviction proceedings, tenancies or defaults that predate it or are pending when it takes effect, or is the matter governed by the earlier or general law?
question_b: Can a person claim a statutory tenancy or sub-tenancy protection (security of tenure, protected-tenant or occupancy status, or protection from eviction) when the governing statute expressly or by its definition excludes the claimant's class, the lessor, or the land from that protection?
note: The rules mostly address different issues (temporal reach of a legal change versus statutory coverage and exclusion), but they overlap where a protective law lapses or is repealed: Rule A would keep accrued rights and pending proceedings under the earlier law, while Rule B's 'no longer in force' limb denies protection. The likely explanation is an unstated difference such as a saving or transitional provision, or whether the Act was temporary, which separates the outcomes.

question_a: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
question_b: Once an appealable remand order has gone unappealed, or a prior decision or review has become final, can a court in later proceedings (on remand, in a later appeal, or on review or a post-judgment motion) reopen or re-examine the correctness of that earlier determination directly or indirectly, including through inherent powers?
note: Rule A limits a High Court's power to reappraise factual findings in revisional, supervisory or second-appellate jurisdiction, while Rule B bars reopening finally settled or unappealed determinations in later proceedings, so they address distinct legal questions and can be applied together without conflict.

question_a: Is a court or rent controller bound to strike out a tenant's defence automatically whenever the tenant fails to pay or deposit rent as ordered in an eviction proceeding, or does it have discretion to retain the defence and condone the default, and when should that discretion be exercised for or against the tenant?
question_b: Under rent-control legislation (principally s.10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 and its analogues), when is a tenant's non-payment of rent a 'wilful default' justifying eviction, and how do the landlord's two-month notice and the tenant's circumstances affect that finding?
note: Rule A governs the procedural consequence (striking out the defence) of breaching an in-proceeding order to pay or deposit rent, while Rule B governs the substantive eviction ground of 'wilful default' in paying rent under rent-control statutes, so they answer different legal questions even though both concern tenant non-payment.

question_a: When can an application to set aside an execution sale (by deposit under Order 21 Rule 89 or by challenge under Rule 90 and analogous provisions) be entertained or allowed, and what effect do the deposit requirement, its timing and compliance, and the structure of the application have on the sale?
question_b: When a judgment-debtor applies under Order XXI Rule 89 CPC to set aside an execution sale, must the required deposit be made within 30 days of the sale (Order XXI Rule 92(2)), or is a deposit made within the longer 60-day application period under Article 127 of the Limitation Act sufficient?
note: Rule A is the general principle that a full and timely deposit is a condition precedent, and Rule B narrows it by saying what counts as 'timely' (the 60-day Article 127 period rather than the 30-day Rule 92(2) period), so the two are consistent unless A's 'in time' is read as strictly 30 days, which A does not state.

question_a: Can a High Court, in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, set aside concurrent (or first appellate) findings of fact by reappreciating the evidence when no substantial question of law arises and the findings are supported by evidence and not perverse?
question_b: When may an appellate, revisional or supervisory court (including the Supreme Court under Article 136) interfere with a lower court's discretionary decision, and when must it leave that decision undisturbed?
note: Rule A limits a High Court's statutory power under Section 100 CPC to reappreciate evidence and disturb factual findings, while Rule B governs when a higher court may interfere with a lower court's discretionary orders, so they address different questions even though both express appellate restraint.

question_a: Does a person who qualifies as a tenant under a protective tenancy or rent-control statute keep tenant status and protection against eviction after a general-law event (expiry of a fixed term, termination, an eviction decree, absence of an allotment order, or the lessor's death), so that eviction is possible only on a statutory ground and through the prescribed process?
question_b: When a party (landlord, tenant or pre-emptor) dies while a suit, application or appeal is pending, does the right to sue or the eviction claim survive so that successors can continue or defend it?
note: Rule A asks whether statutory tenant status and protection continue after a general-law event ends the tenancy, while Rule B asks whether a claim survives a party's death during pending proceedings, so they address distinct questions and do not produce inconsistent outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Does a landlord's acceptance of rent or equivalent payments after a lease or tenancy has expired or been terminated create a new tenancy by holding over, or waive a termination notice or eviction ground, in the absence of the landlord's clear assent to continued possession or intention to treat the lease as subsisting?
question_b: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
note: Rule A asks whether a landlord's acceptance of rent after a tenancy ends creates a new tenancy or waives a notice or eviction ground, while Rule B asks whether a tenant can use general property-law protections such as relief against forfeiture or a right to sublet against a statutory rent-control eviction ground, so the two rules address distinct questions and cannot produce opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: When an appellate decree is compared as a whole with the trial court's decision as a whole, does it count as a decree of affirmance, and which kinds of variation (merits, interest, costs, concession or consent, favourable or unfavourable to the would-be appellant) change that character?
question_b: When the law changes while an appeal or other proceeding is pending, must the appellate court decide it under the changed law, or does the earlier law (or a vested right) continue to govern?
note: Rule A decides whether an appellate decree counts as one of affirmance, based on whether the appellate court varied the trial decision on the merits, while Rule B decides which law (changed or earlier) governs a pending appeal, so the questions and outcomes do not overlap.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction be sustained when the prosecution's key evidence (eyewitness, sole-witness, dying declaration, approver or confession evidence) is materially unreliable because of contradictions, improvements, interest or hostility, conflict with medical or other evidence, or investigative lapses, and there is no reliable independent corroboration to leave guilt proved beyond reasonable doubt?
question_b: When may a court decline to rely on a confession (extra-judicial or by a co-accused) as evidence of guilt or as corroboration, because its credibility, voluntariness, procedural fairness or independence is in doubt?
