note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent application of Rule A's logic to confession evidence (one type of key evidence): it says when a court will not rely on a confession, while Rule A says when a conviction resting on unreliable key evidence without independent corroboration must be set aside.

question_a: When a claimant invokes the discretionary writ jurisdiction of a constitutional court after substantial delay, can relief be refused for laches, and what circumstances (explanation for the delay, third-party rights, the nature of the interest) decide the point?
question_b: Will the Supreme Court, on appeal, interfere with or accept a procedural-timeliness or alternative-remedy objection (delay, laches, or an available statutory remedy) where the court or authority below exercised its discretion to entertain the proceeding and the objection was not pressed or the delay was explained?
note: Rule B is the appellate-stage application of the deference principle in the last sentence of Rule A (the Supreme Court will not disturb the forum below's discretionary handling of delay), while Rule A's permissive 'may be refused' for unexplained delay does not contradict it.

question_a: Does a statutory bar on civil suits or on challenges to a sale or an administrative decision (a jurisdiction bar, a limitation bar, or a bar on benami-type claims) apply when the claim or sale falls outside the bar's defined scope, for example because the authority lacked jurisdiction, the grounds are different, no lawful sale occurred, or the prescribed certificate was never issued?
question_b: Does a statutory provision barring courts from questioning orders made under the Act (or excluding civil suits) prevent a court from examining an order that was made without jurisdiction, outside the statute, or in breach of fundamental procedure or natural justice?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent application of Rule A's principle that a statutory bar applies only within its terms: ouster clauses protect only valid orders within jurisdiction and do not shield jurisdictional defects, ultra vires acts, or natural-justice breaches, whereas Rule A covers a wider range of bars (limitation, benami, sale-related) and preconditions.

question_a: Can a party, or the appellate court itself, rely on a factual contention, defence or case that was not pleaded, not made the subject of an issue and not tried in the courts below, when it is raised for the first time on appeal?
question_b: Can an appellate or revisional court rely on additional or fresh evidence (documents, account books or other material) that was not admitted and proved in accordance with law, or that the affected party had no opportunity to challenge or rebut?
note: Rule A bars new unpleaded factual cases or defences raised for the first time on appeal, while Rule B governs when an appellate or revisional court may rely on additional or unproved evidence, so they address distinct questions (pleadings and issues versus admission, proof and opportunity to rebut evidence) and neither is a narrower form of the other or yields conflicting outcomes.

question_a: Can a High Court decide a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in particular by reappreciating evidence and reversing the factual findings of the courts below, without first formulating a substantial question of law and hearing the appeal on that question?
question_b: When may or should an appellate court remand a matter to the court below for determination, and when must it instead decide the appeal itself on the existing record?
note: Rule A concerns the High Court's jurisdiction to decide a second appeal under Section 100 CPC only on a formulated substantial question of law, while Rule B concerns the general, discretionary power of appellate courts to remand, and the only overlap is that remand is one possible remedy under Rule A, which does not make the two rules answer the same question or produce inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: Does a transfer of land acquire no validity, and convey no title to the transferee, where the transferor lacked title or the transfer contravened a statutory or grant-based restriction, prohibition or vesting?
question_b: When is a compulsory land acquisition, or an action built on it, invalid because the power was used for an extraneous or private purpose, or because the notification or procedure did not meet the statutory requirements for the stated purpose?
note: Rule A asks whether a private transfer of land conveys title when the transferor lacked title or breached a statutory or grant restriction, whereas Rule B asks whether a compulsory acquisition or action founded on it is invalid for an extraneous purpose or failure to meet statutory requirements, so they address different questions and do not produce opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: What is the effect of the prosecution's failure to explain injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence: does it require rejection of, or reasonable doubt about, the prosecution case, or can the case stand where the injuries are minor or the prosecution evidence is clear, cogent and credible?
question_b: Does the prosecution's failure to examine a particular witness (or to record or produce some item of evidence) by itself undermine the prosecution case or justify an adverse inference, where the evidence actually led is reliable and no prejudice or improper withholding of an essential witness is shown?
note: Rule A concerns the effect of the prosecution's failure to explain an accused's injuries sustained in the same occurrence, while Rule B concerns whether non-examination of a witness or evidence undermines the prosecution case, so they address distinct questions and do not yield conflicting outcomes.

question_a: Does a special summary eviction procedure for unauthorised occupants of public (government or municipal) premises violate the Article 14 equality guarantee because it differs from the procedure for private premises, or because an ordinary civil remedy is also available?
question_b: Does a law governing property, housing, rent or premises violate the Article 14 guarantee of equality merely because it treats different categories of property, premises, tenants or buildings differently, where the categories rest on an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the law's object?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B's general Article 14 reasonable-classification test to special eviction procedures for public premises, and both reach consistent outcomes (the classification is upheld where it has a rational nexus to the law's object).

question_a: Must a first appellate court (or other appellate authority) deciding an appeal on fact and law independently assess the evidence, decide the material issues, and give reasons, engaging with the trial court's reasoning where it reverses, and what is the consequence of failing to do so?
question_b: Must a court deciding a contested issue, application, appeal or supervisory challenge give reasons that show it applied its mind to the material contentions or findings, and is an unreasoned order unsustainable?
note: Rule A is a narrower special case of Rule B, applying the general duty to give reasons to first appellate courts (independent assessment of evidence, deciding material issues, engaging with reversed trial findings), and both reach the same outcome of setting aside and remanding for a fresh reasoned decision.

question_a: When may the Supreme Court, hearing an appeal (typically by special leave under Article 136), disturb concurrent findings of fact reached by the trial court and the appellate or High Court?
question_b: When may a higher court (second appellate, revisional, writ or special-leave court) interfere with concurrent or supported findings of fact by rent or eviction fact-finding authorities on matters such as the landlord's bona fide need, comparative hardship, acquiescence or fair rent?
note: Rule B applies the general Rule A principle of non-interference with evidence-based concurrent factual findings to the narrower setting of rent or eviction proceedings, with consistent outcomes and materially the same exceptions (perversity, legal error, other sufficient ground).

question_a: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
question_b: Where premises are let for both residential and non-residential (professional or business) purposes, or a residential letting is openly used for non-residential purposes with the landlord's consent, can the landlord evict on a ground that depends on the premises being residential (landlord's residential need, or tenant's acquisition of other residence)?
note: Rule A asks whether a separate notice terminating the tenancy is needed before eviction, while Rule B asks whether a residence-based eviction ground is available for a mixed-use or consented non-residential letting, so the questions and outcomes do not overlap.

question_a: Is a person or body that has a direct or indirect interest in acquired or requisitioned property or its compensation (such as a beneficiary bearing the compensation, a purchaser, decree-holder, tenant, allottee or administrator) treated as a person interested, with standing to be joined, to receive notice, to lead evidence and to challenge adverse orders or awards?
question_b: What must the statutory objection-and-hearing procedure before a compulsory land acquisition (chiefly Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894) provide, and what follows when the procedure is or is not complied with?
note: Rule A decides who counts as a 'person interested' with standing to be heard and to challenge compensation or acquisition orders, whereas Rule B decides what the s.5A objection hearing must involve and the effect of non-compliance, so they address distinct legal questions with no outcome overlap.

question_a: Is a civil court's jurisdiction under Section 9 CPC excluded, expressly or by necessary implication, where a special land-related statute assigns the matter in dispute (or a question on which the relief depends) to a designated authority, revenue court or special forum and provides finality or remedies there?
question_b: Can a protected tenant be evicted, or possession decreed against them, other than through the forum and procedure laid down by the rent-control or tenancy statute and on a statutory ground that the court has found, or has material to find, established?
note: Rule B is a narrower application of Rule A's forum-exclusivity principle to rent-control and tenancy statutes: an ordinary civil suit cannot evict a protected occupant, because the statute assigns that matter to a designated forum. Rule B also adds a merits requirement, that a statutory ground be established, and the two rules never give opposite outcomes.

question_a: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
question_b: When a landlord or authority proceeds for eviction on a particular statutory ground or under a special statutory procedure, is it excused from satisfying a further prerequisite or protection (such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of title, a rehousing duty or tenant-protection law) because that requirement is not part of the invoked ground or is displaced by the invoked scheme?
note: Rule A is a narrower application of Rule B's principle: in a rent-control eviction on a statutory ground, an extra protection from general property law (relief against forfeiture, a default right to sublet) is not part of the invoked scheme and is displaced by it, so the tenant cannot invoke it, and the outcomes are consistent.

question_a: Must a first appellate court (or other appellate authority) deciding an appeal on fact and law independently assess the evidence, decide the material issues, and give reasons, engaging with the trial court's reasoning where it reverses, and what is the consequence of failing to do so?
question_b: Where a court exercises a limited jurisdiction (review, writ/certiorari, supervisory or appellate-on-facts), may it reappraise evidence or reconsider the merits, or must it confine itself to jurisdictional defects and errors apparent on the face of the record?
note: Rule A sets the duty of a full first appellate court to assess evidence independently and give reasons, while Rule B limits courts with restricted jurisdiction (review, writ, supervisory) from reappraising merits; the two are complementary, since a first appellate court's failure under Rule A would itself count as a legal defect that Rule B allows a limited-jurisdiction court to correct.

question_a: In a rent-control eviction proceeding founded on the landlord's bona fide need, how must the court decide the statutory limits on eviction (comparative hardship, tenant protection, partial eviction and related relief) once the need is established, and what must it consider before ordering full eviction?
question_b: In a summary eviction proceeding where the tenant must obtain leave to contest or defend, when must the Controller or court grant leave, and when may it refuse leave?
note: Rule A governs how the court must decide comparative hardship, partial eviction and tenant protection after bona fide need is established, while Rule B governs the earlier procedural question of when a tenant must be granted leave to contest in summary eviction, so the two address different questions and can operate together without producing inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
question_b: Can a High Court decide a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in particular by reappreciating evidence and reversing the factual findings of the courts below, without first formulating a substantial question of law and hearing the appeal on that question?
note: Rule B applies Rule A's bar on reappreciating evidence to the specific setting of a Section 100 CPC second appeal, adding a procedural requirement (formulating a substantial question of law) and treating a breach as a want of jurisdiction, with no inconsistent outcome.

question_a: When may a High Court, in second appeal (or analogous revision), interfere with or reappraise the factual findings of the lower courts, including concurrent findings, and when must it leave them undisturbed?
question_b: When may an appellate, revisional or supervisory court (including the Supreme Court under Article 136) interfere with a lower court's discretionary decision, and when must it leave that decision undisturbed?
note: Rule A governs when a High Court in second appeal may disturb factual findings (needing a substantial question of law), while Rule B governs when a higher court may disturb a lower court's discretionary decision; both use a perversity-type threshold, but they cover different subject matter and do not produce contradictory outcomes.

question_a: Can a claimant obtain declaratory, injunctive, possessory or other property-related relief when the claimant has not established the foundational right on which the relief depends, such as title, actual or lawful possession, a lawful interest, or a legal status?
question_b: Can a person claim statutory tenancy or land-rights protection (tenant, deemed tenant, adhivasi, landholder or retention rights) on the basis of a tenancy, lease or cultivatory possession that was invalid, unlawful or granted by someone with no right or authority to grant it?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent application of Rule A: a statutory tenancy or land-rights claim is a property-related claim, and when the required foundational right (valid tenancy or lawful possession) is not established, the claim fails.

question_a: Does a landlord's acceptance of rent or equivalent payments after a lease or tenancy has expired or been terminated create a new tenancy by holding over, or waive a termination notice or eviction ground, in the absence of the landlord's clear assent to continued possession or intention to treat the lease as subsisting?
question_b: In an eviction proceeding founded on rent default, does the outcome depend on whether the tenant followed the payment, deposit or demand procedure prescribed by the rent statute, and is the consequence of non-compliance limited to what the statute provides rather than being automatic eviction?
note: Rule A asks whether a landlord's acceptance of post-termination rent creates a new tenancy or waives a notice or eviction ground, while Rule B asks what consequence follows when a tenant fails to follow the statutory payment, deposit or demand procedure in a rent-default eviction, so they address distinct questions and give no conflicting outcomes.

question_a: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
question_b: Where a statute provides a specific remedy or procedure for a claimed right (adjustment or refund of excess rent, or restoration of possession to a tenant), can the party bypass it by relying on an automatic or general-law set-off, or on a summary procedure?
note: Both rules reflect the idea that rent-control statutes are self-contained, but Rule A asks whether tenants can import property-law doctrines (relief against forfeiture, a default right to sublet) while Rule B asks whether a party can bypass a specific statutory remedy or procedure (excess-rent adjustment, restoration of possession) through set-off or a summary route, so they answer different questions and never produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: Is a special acquisition, town-planning or improvement scheme invalid under the equality guarantee (Article 14) merely because its procedure, compensation method or review mechanism differs from the general land-acquisition law, or because another acquisition law could theoretically be used?
question_b: Can solatium (and interest) be denied to owners of compulsorily acquired land merely because the land is acquired under a special or different enactment, for a different public purpose or by a different authority, rather than under the general land-acquisition law?
note: Both apply the Article 14 rational-basis test to special acquisition regimes, and Rule B is the narrower application to omitted solatium and interest, where a difference based only on statute, purpose or authority fails, which is consistent with Rule A upholding differences that have a rational basis and a reasonable compensation mechanism.

question_a: Is a civil court's jurisdiction (or a later civil suit) barred by a special tenancy, revenue, rent-control or similar statute or forum, or by that forum's earlier decision, where the forum was not empowered to decide the matter or grant the relief claimed?
question_b: When a question that tenancy legislation assigns exclusively to a special authority or forum arises in a civil suit that was properly instituted, must the civil court refer or direct that question to the competent forum, instead of deciding it itself or dismissing the suit outright?
note: Rule A decides whether a civil court is barred at all (no, if the special forum lacked power and no statute ousts the court), while Rule B governs what a civil court must do once a bar over a specific issue is established (refer or redirect, not decide or dismiss), so their conditions are mutually exclusive and they never produce conflicting outcomes.

question_a: When an appellate court finds that material factual or title/possession questions in a land or property dispute remain unresolved because of an inadequate record, procedural error or erroneous reasoning below, should it remand the matter for fresh determination rather than decide it finally?
question_b: When a lower court or revisional or supervisory authority has not decided a material issue on the merits, or has decided it on an incomplete or unclear footing, may the appellate court set aside the decision and remand the matter for a fresh decision?
note: Rule A is the land/property-dispute application of Rule B's general power to remand when a material issue was left undecided or decided on a defective footing, and its futility exception matches Rule B's 'fresh determination necessary' condition, so the two are consistent.

question_a: What is the effect of the prosecution's failure to explain injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence: does it require rejection of, or reasonable doubt about, the prosecution case, or can the case stand where the injuries are minor or the prosecution evidence is clear, cogent and credible?
question_b: Does the acquittal of some co-accused, or the rejection of part of a witness's evidence, require the court to acquit the remaining accused or reject the rest of the evidence, where the evidence against the remaining accused is credible and can be separated from the rejected part?
note: Rule A asks whether the prosecution's failure to explain an accused's injuries undermines its case, while Rule B asks whether acquitting some co-accused or rejecting part of a witness's testimony compels acquittal of the rest, so the two address distinct questions and do not produce conflicting outcomes.

question_a: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?
question_b: Where a landlord sues (or applies) to recover possession from a tenant, does limitation run from the proved determination or termination of the tenancy under the specific provision for landlord-tenant recovery, so that a filing within the period counted from that point is not time-barred?
note: Rule A asks whether a separate termination notice is needed before eviction, while Rule B asks when limitation runs and whether a possession suit is time-barred, so they address distinct questions and their outcomes do not contradict each other.

question_a: Can an accused be held liable for murder on the basis of constructive liability (common intention under Section 34 or common object of an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC) for a fatal act of another, where the evidence does not establish that murder was the shared intention or common object, or that the accused knew murder was likely in prosecution of the common object?
question_b: When can a participant in a group assault that causes death be held jointly liable under Section 34 IPC (common intention) on the basis of intention inferred from the circumstances, even without a prior plan or proof of that participant's own fatal act, and when is that liability limited to a lesser offence or excluded?
note: Rule A states the general limit on constructive liability for murder under Sections 34 and 149 (no liability without proof of shared murderous intention, common object or known likelihood), while Rule B is the narrower, consistent Section 34 application where shared intention to cause the fatal harm is inferred from the circumstances of a joint attack, so the two give the same outcome on any given facts.

question_a: Can a claimant obtain declaratory, injunctive, possessory or other property-related relief when the claimant has not established the foundational right on which the relief depends, such as title, actual or lawful possession, a lawful interest, or a legal status?
question_b: Does a party who seeks relief founded on title, possession or another asserted right bear the burden of proving that right, including the identity of the property, without relying on the opponent's failure to prove a competing title?
note: Both rules deny relief to a claimant who fails to prove the right it rests on, but Rule B is the narrower burden-of-proof application (title and property identity, no reliance on the opponent's weak title), while Rule A is the broader principle covering injunctions, status and other property-related relief.

question_a: Can a person who is not the owner or a successful party at the relevant time (a purchaser or transferee after the acquisition notification, or a non-objector or non-party relying on others' successful challenges or on defects affecting others) challenge the acquisition or claim title, policy benefits or relief against the acquiring State, or is such a person limited to compensation through the former owner?
question_b: When is a compulsory land acquisition, or an action built on it, invalid because the power was used for an extraneous or private purpose, or because the notification or procedure did not meet the statutory requirements for the stated purpose?
note: Rule A is about who has standing to challenge an acquisition or claim benefits (post-notification transferees and non-objectors are limited to compensation), while Rule B is about the substantive grounds on which an acquisition is invalid (extraneous purpose or unmet statutory requirements), so they can both apply to the same case without contradicting each other.

question_a: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?
question_b: Does an existing tenancy or subordinate interest continue despite an intervening event (partial acquisition of the reversion, merger of interests, statutory abolition or vesting, a termination notice or pending possession proceeding, a third-party title suit, or wrongful dispossession) that does not satisfy the legally prescribed requirements for ending it?
note: Rule A asks whether a tenant can import general property-law defences (relief against forfeiture, a default right to sublet) against a statutory eviction ground, while Rule B asks whether a tenancy survives intervening events that do not meet the legal requirements for termination, so they address distinct questions and do not produce inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: Can a High Court, in revisional, supervisory (Art. 226/227) or second-appellate jurisdiction, set aside a subordinate court's or tribunal's supported factual finding (especially concurrent findings) by reappreciating the evidence and preferring a different view, when no jurisdictional error, perversity, absence of evidence or other error of law is shown?
question_b: Must a first appellate court (or other appellate authority) deciding an appeal on fact and law independently assess the evidence, decide the material issues, and give reasons, engaging with the trial court's reasoning where it reverses, and what is the consequence of failing to do so?
note: Rule A limits a High Court's power to reappraise facts in revisional, supervisory or second-appellate jurisdiction, while Rule B sets the duty of a first appellate court to assess evidence independently and give reasons, so they govern different forums and are complementary, not contradictory.

question_a: Under rent-control legislation, when does a tenant's act (subletting without the required consent, use contrary to the lease, or construction or alteration of the premises) establish a statutory ground for eviction, and what must the landlord prove?
question_b: When does a tenant's handing over of premises to another person (a relative, a business entity, a dealer or a company) amount to subletting or parting with possession, so that the statutory ground for eviction or the denial of tenant protection is made out?
note: Rule B narrows the subletting limb of Rule A by defining when handing over premises counts as subletting or parting with possession (exclusive possession, no retained legal control), which is consistent with Rule A's requirement that the landlord prove every statutory element.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction be sustained when the prosecution's key evidence (eyewitness, sole-witness, dying declaration, approver or confession evidence) is materially unreliable because of contradictions, improvements, interest or hostility, conflict with medical or other evidence, or investigative lapses, and there is no reliable independent corroboration to leave guilt proved beyond reasonable doubt?
question_b: Where the prosecution's evidence is affected by unexplained procedural or evidentiary defects (such as unexplained delay in lodging or forwarding the FIR, discrepancies, withheld witnesses, or doubtful official/independent witnesses), is the prosecution case unreliable and therefore not proved beyond reasonable doubt so as to preclude conviction?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent subset of Rule A: it covers unexplained procedural defects (FIR delay, withheld witnesses, doubtful official witnesses) as one source of unreliable key evidence, and like Rule A it leads to reasonable doubt and no safe conviction when there is no explanation or corroboration.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: When a law authorising compulsory acquisition or requisition of property is challenged on the ground that its compensation is inadequate or illusory, is the challenge open to judicial review, and what must the compensation provisions satisfy to survive it?
note: Rule B is the narrower compensation-specific case: its saving-provision branch applies Rule A's immunity from Part III challenge to compensation claims (keeping legislative-competence challenges outside), and its second branch covers unprotected laws, which Rule A does not address, so the outcomes are consistent.

question_a: When can an accused who pleads private defence (of person or property) establish that right, given who was the aggressor, whether there was a reasonable apprehension of danger, the weapons carried, the injuries on each side, and the credibility of the defence account?
question_b: Can an accused who goes to land in another party's possession and initiates or escalates an assault on those resisting or objecting claim a right of private defence of person or property?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent special case of Rule A: it covers the situation where the accused enter another's possessed land over objection and initiate or pursue the assault, which is one of Rule A's 'accused were aggressors' triggers, and both reach the same outcome of private defence not being available.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: Is a state law that acquires or vests land, minerals or an undertaking invalid for want of legislative competence or for repugnancy to a central law on a related subject (planning, mining, forests, industry control, electricity or land acquisition), where the two laws have different dominant purposes and can operate together?
note: Rule A asks whether Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B shield a land or estate law from Part III fundamental-rights challenges, while Rule B asks whether a state law is valid on legislative competence or repugnancy grounds under the Seventh Schedule, so the two address distinct legal questions and can both apply to the same statute without giving different outcomes.

question_a: Once a compensation determination, payment or related direction in land-acquisition matters has become final or been satisfied at an earlier stage, can it be reopened, recalled or reappropriated in later proceedings (reference, appeal, execution or fresh acquisition proceedings)?
question_b: Can a final land-acquisition compensation award or decree be reopened, whether by redetermination or by a later application for additional statutory benefits, when the applicant has no statutory basis for doing so, such as a prior reference, a missed limitation period, or a request beyond mere correction?
note: Both rules protect the finality of land-acquisition compensation, but Rule A bars reopening unless the earlier order is void or a court directs otherwise, while Rule B permits reopening through express statutory remedies such as section 28A or correction and treats any court-directed reopening outside them as void, so the outcomes differ on those facts and the difference turns on a statutory-remedy distinction that Rule A does not state.

question_a: In an eviction proceeding founded on rent default, does the outcome depend on whether the tenant followed the payment, deposit or demand procedure prescribed by the rent statute, and is the consequence of non-compliance limited to what the statute provides rather than being automatic eviction?
question_b: Under rent-control legislation (principally s.10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 and its analogues), when is a tenant's non-payment of rent a 'wilful default' justifying eviction, and how do the landlord's two-month notice and the tenant's circumstances affect that finding?
note: Rule A asks what consequence follows when a tenant departs from a statutory payment, deposit or demand procedure (only the statutory consequence, not automatic eviction), while Rule B asks when non-payment counts as 'wilful default' under s.10(2)(i) and its analogues, so the two address distinct questions and can be applied together without contradiction.

question_a: Under rent-control legislation, when does a tenant's act (subletting without the required consent, use contrary to the lease, or construction or alteration of the premises) establish a statutory ground for eviction, and what must the landlord prove?
question_b: Where premises are let for both residential and non-residential (professional or business) purposes, or a residential letting is openly used for non-residential purposes with the landlord's consent, can the landlord evict on a ground that depends on the premises being residential (landlord's residential need, or tenant's acquisition of other residence)?
note: Rule A covers when a tenant's act (unauthorised subletting, misuse, or damaging construction) makes out an eviction ground, while Rule B covers whether residence-based grounds (landlord's residential need, tenant's other residence) are available for mixed-use or consented non-residential lettings, so they address different grounds and cannot yield opposing outcomes on the same facts.

question_a: Does the prosecution's failure to examine a particular witness (or to record or produce some item of evidence) by itself undermine the prosecution case or justify an adverse inference, where the evidence actually led is reliable and no prejudice or improper withholding of an essential witness is shown?
question_b: Does the acquittal of some co-accused, or the rejection of part of a witness's evidence, require the court to acquit the remaining accused or reject the rest of the evidence, where the evidence against the remaining accused is credible and can be separated from the rejected part?
note: Rule A asks whether the prosecution's non-examination of a witness or evidence weakens its case or supports an adverse inference, while Rule B asks whether acquitting some co-accused or rejecting part of a witness's testimony requires acquitting the rest, so the questions and triggering facts differ and no facts would produce conflicting outcomes.

question_a: Can a criminal conviction rest on credible eyewitness testimony, including testimony from injured, related or partisan witnesses, when it is consistent, carefully scrutinised and corroborated by medical or other evidence, and when discrepancies, relationship, investigative omissions or the accused's injuries are alleged to undermine it?
question_b: Can a conviction rest on reliable in-court identification of the accused where a test identification parade was not held, failed, or is of little value, and what corroboration or reliability is needed?
note: Rule A asks whether a conviction can rest on credible eyewitness testimony of the offence (presence, consistency, corroboration, and the effect of relationship or discrepancies), while Rule B asks whether in-court identification of the accused can establish identity without a valid test identification parade; the two can both apply in one case but they answer different questions and never give opposing outcomes.

question_a: When a party who won below (or who did not appeal) is respondent in an appeal, may it support the decree on grounds or findings decided against it without filing its own appeal or cross-objection, and when must it appeal or cross-object?
question_b: Can a court decide an issue or grant relief on a ground that was not specifically pleaded or framed as an issue, where the parties understood the matter was in dispute, had an opportunity to lead evidence on it, and suffered no prejudice or surprise?
note: Rule A concerns whether a respondent holding a favourable decree may defend it on adverse findings without filing an appeal or cross-objection (Order 41 Rule 22 CPC procedure), while Rule B concerns whether a court may decide a matter not specifically pleaded or framed as an issue when parties understood it and suffered no prejudice, so they address distinct questions and cannot yield conflicting outcomes.

question_a: When is a preliminary land-acquisition notification (and the related declaration) sufficient, or invalid for vagueness or inadequate notice? Specifically, does it adequately indicate the public purpose and identify the land so that interested persons can understand the proposal and object, without having to state further matters such as the executing instrumentality or the company route, or to give individual notice?
question_b: Is a public purpose for acquisition (or for later disposal of acquired land) valid and sufficiently specific when it is stated in general terms, such as planned development, housing or industrial and residential development, for a large area, so long as it serves the community or common good?
note: Rule B elaborates one element of Rule A (the 'public purpose adequately indicated' condition) by holding that general-terms purposes like planned development or housing suffice for large-area acquisitions, and the two rules give consistent outcomes, although B also covers disposal of acquired land, which A does not address.

question_a: Does a mining or other lessee have an enforceable right to renewal, extension or grant of a lease, or is the claim defeated where no such right arises from the lease terms, statute or rules, the lessor lacked authority or rights, or the required statutory conditions and reasons were not met?
question_b: Must mining operations, including new leases, renewals, fresh grants and small minor-mineral leases, hold a prior environmental clearance under the EIA notifications, and can that requirement be displaced by earlier clearances, approved mining plans, administrative circulars, or later clearances?
note: Rule A asks whether a lessee has an enforceable right to renewal, extension or grant (generally not, unless the lease, statute or rules confer one), while Rule B asks whether a grant or renewal is lawful without prior environmental clearance; the two address different questions and can both apply to the same renewal without producing inconsistent outcomes.

question_a: Can a party, or the appellate court itself, rely on a factual contention, defence or case that was not pleaded, not made the subject of an issue and not tried in the courts below, when it is raised for the first time on appeal?
question_b: When a party who won below (or who did not appeal) is respondent in an appeal, may it support the decree on grounds or findings decided against it without filing its own appeal or cross-objection, and when must it appeal or cross-object?
note: Rule A asks whether a new, unpleaded and untried factual case can be raised on appeal, while Rule B asks whether a respondent defending its own favourable decree needs a cross-objection, so the two address separate questions and can be applied together without conflict.

question_a: When a landlord or authority proceeds for eviction on a particular statutory ground or under a special statutory procedure, is it excused from satisfying a further prerequisite or protection (such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of title, a rehousing duty or tenant-protection law) because that requirement is not part of the invoked ground or is displaced by the invoked scheme?
question_b: Where premises are let for both residential and non-residential (professional or business) purposes, or a residential letting is openly used for non-residential purposes with the landlord's consent, can the landlord evict on a ground that depends on the premises being residential (landlord's residential need, or tenant's acquisition of other residence)?
note: Rule A asks whether a requirement outside the invoked eviction ground or scheme can be excused once that ground's conditions are met, while Rule B asks whether a residence-based ground's own condition (residential character of the letting) is met in composite or consented non-residential tenancies, so they address distinct questions and do not yield conflicting outcomes.

question_a: When may a High Court, in second appeal (or analogous revision), interfere with or reappraise the factual findings of the lower courts, including concurrent findings, and when must it leave them undisturbed?
question_b: When may a High Court set aside an acquittal (on appeal or in revision) and order a retrial or continuation of the trial, and what kind of defect in the acquittal or the trial is needed to justify it?
note: Rule A governs when a High Court may disturb lower-court factual findings in civil second appeal or analogous revision, while Rule B governs when a High Court may set aside an acquittal and order retrial in criminal proceedings, so they address different questions, although both bar mere reappraisal of evidence.

question_a: When is a later suit for a claim or relief barred because it was omitted from an earlier suit on the same cause of action (Order II Rule 2 CPC), and what proceedings fall outside that bar?
question_b: Is a party barred, by res judicata or constructive res judicata, from bringing a later writ or constitutional challenge that either repeats a matter already decided or raises a ground that was available and could and ought to have been raised in an earlier proceeding on the same cause of action?
note: Rule A concerns the Order II Rule 2 CPC bar on later suits for claims or reliefs omitted without leave (whether the earlier suit is pending or decided), while Rule B concerns res judicata and constructive res judicata in later writ or constitutional proceedings after a final decision, so they cover different proceedings and different doctrines without producing conflicting outcomes.

question_a: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?
question_b: Is a compulsory acquisition that was made for a public purpose invalidated by a collateral, prior, subsequent or extraneous circumstance, such as a later diversion or release of the land, an earlier abandoned or alternative proceeding, the owner's existing or intended use, a plan or land-use mismatch, a failed negotiation, or a procedural or record irregularity, when no defect in the statutory acquisition process or the public purpose itself is shown?
note: Rule A asks whether Articles 31(4), 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule bar Part III fundamental-rights challenges to estate-reform or scheduled laws, while Rule B asks whether collateral or extraneous circumstances invalidate an otherwise valid public-purpose acquisition, so they address different legal questions and do not produce opposing outcomes.

question_a: When may a court rely on testimony that is inherently suspect or partial (an approver's or accomplice's evidence, a retracted confession, a hostile witness's evidence, or the evidence of an interested or sole witness) to convict an accused, and what scrutiny and corroboration does it require?
question_b: Does the acquittal of some co-accused, or the rejection of part of a witness's evidence, require the court to acquit the remaining accused or reject the rest of the evidence, where the evidence against the remaining accused is credible and can be separated from the rejected part?
note: Rule A asks what scrutiny and corroboration are needed before suspect or partial testimony can support a conviction, while Rule B asks whether acquitting some accused or rejecting part of a witness's evidence forces acquittal of the others; B only says such rejection is not automatically fatal, so it does not contradict A's corroboration requirement even where both apply, as with a partly rejected hostile or interested witness.

question_a: Is a judgment, decree or judicial order obtained by fraud or collusion on the court a nullity that can be challenged, recalled or set aside, including in collateral proceedings, despite finality, res judicata or other procedural bars?
question_b: Does a statutory bar on civil-court jurisdiction or on separate suits (a special-statute bar, the bar on suits against compromise decrees, or the arbitration-law bar) prevent a challenge to a decree or order alleged to have been obtained by fraud or collusion?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent application of Rule A's fraud-on-court principle to the specific situation where a statutory bar on civil-court jurisdiction or separate suits is raised, holding that such bars do not defeat the challenge at the threshold.

question_a: Are the benefits introduced by the 1984 amendment to the Land Acquisition Act (additional amount under s.23(1-A), enhanced solatium under s.23(2), and related interest or limits) available where the Collector's award, and in some cases the reference court's award, was made before the amendment's transitional threshold, even though an appeal, revision or reference remains pending or is decided after the amendment took effect?
question_b: Can a final land-acquisition compensation award or decree be reopened, whether by redetermination or by a later application for additional statutory benefits, when the applicant has no statutory basis for doing so, such as a prior reference, a missed limitation period, or a request beyond mere correction?
note: Rule A asks whether the 1984 amendment's benefits apply retrospectively to proceedings whose Collector's award predates the transitional threshold, while Rule B asks whether a final award can be reopened without an express statutory remedy, so the questions differ and the outcomes never contradict each other.

question_a: Where a transfer of immovable property must be made by a registered instrument, can an oral sale, an agreement or contract to sell, an unregistered document, or delivery of possession alone transfer title or create an interest in the property before a registered conveyance is completed?
question_b: Can a person in possession of immovable property under an agreement to sell rely on the doctrine of part performance (Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act) to retain possession when the statutory requirements are not established, and can such a person also claim title by adverse possession?
note: Rule B is a narrower, consistent application of Rule A: it covers the possession-under-agreement-to-sell scenario and holds that Section 53A gives only a limited defensive shield, available when all its requirements are proved, and never title, which matches Rule A's holding that an unregistered agreement gives at most a personal right.

question_a: When will the Supreme Court, in an appeal under Article 136 (special leave) or a similar appeal, decline to re-examine or reappraise concurrent or High Court findings of fact?
question_b: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, when may the Supreme Court depart from its ordinary restraint and interfere with, or reappraise, findings of fact, including concurrent findings of the courts below?
note: Rule A states the general restraint (decline to reappraise concurrent findings absent an exceptional ground) and Rule B specifies the exceptional ground (perversity, misread evidence or wrong legal approach, plus grave injustice) that permits interference, so the two are consistent parts of one doctrine, with B elaborating the exception to A.
